tissues.name: Simple squamous epithelium
tissues.summary: Simple squamous epithelium is a single layer of thin, flattened cells that lines blood vessels, body cavities, alveoli and the renal capsule. Its very thin, smooth surface allows rapid diffusion and filtration and reduces friction.
features: Flattened cells in a single layer, with the nucleus bulging into the lumen or cavity
Seen from the surface, cells are thin polygons with pale oval nuclei and dark borders
Endothelium lines vessels; mesothelium lines pleura, pericardium and peritoneum
Also forms type I pneumocytes and the parietal layer of Bowman's capsule
Very thin barrier (under 1 µm) allows rapid gas exchange and filtration

images.title: Simple squamous epithelium: whole mount seen from the surface
images.description: Whole mount of human epithelium at 100x magnification, seen from the surface. The source does not name the stain, but the cells are brown with dark borders. Students should see a sheet of polygonal flat cells, each with a pale oval nucleus, with the staining denser on the left and paler on the right.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Simple squamous epithelium: closer whole mount of surface cells
images.description: Whole mount of human epithelium at 200x magnification, seen from the surface, with the stain not named in the source. The cells are closely packed and polygonal, each with a pale oval nucleus set in speckled brown cytoplasm. Students can compare the cell outlines and nucleus position with the 100x view.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Simple squamous epithelium: high-power surface view of cell borders and nuclei
images.description: Whole mount of human epithelium at 400x magnification, seen from the surface, with the stain not named in the source. Individual cells are clearly outlined, and each has a pale oval nucleus, with thin dark borders where neighbouring cells meet. This is the most detailed of the three whole mounts, so it is the best view for learning the cell outlines.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

tissues.name: Simple cuboidal epithelium
tissues.summary: Simple cuboidal epithelium is a single layer of cube-shaped cells, each with a round central nucleus. It lines small ducts and kidney tubules and is specialised for secretion and absorption.
features: Single layer of cube-shaped cells, about as high as they are wide
Round, central nucleus in the middle of each cell
Cells sit on a thin basement membrane with connective tissue beneath
Lumen lined by the cells, as in kidney tubules, thyroid follicles and small gland ducts
Fuzzy brush border (apical microvilli) on proximal tubule cells, facing the lumen

images.title: Kidney tubules in section: overview of many tubules
images.description: H&E-stained overview of kidney tubules at 100x magnification (the source gives a cross section, but most tubules run lengthways in this view). Each tubule has a pale lumen lined by cells with round nuclei, and loose tissue lies between the tubules. Use it to locate the tubules before looking at the lining cells at higher power.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Kidney tubules with granular material in the lumens
images.description: H&E-stained section of kidney tubules at 200x magnification (the source gives a cross section). Several lumens contain red-brown granular material, and the tubule walls are formed by cuboidal cells with round nuclei. The tissue between the tubules is loose and cellular.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Kidney tubules with pale lumens and cuboidal lining cells
images.description: H&E-stained section of kidney tubules at 200x magnification (the source gives a cross section). Many tubules have pale lumens, and some lumens hold a little pink granular material. Look for the round nuclei of the lining cells and the cellular tissue around the tubules.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Kidney tubules in section with clear lumens
images.description: H&E-stained section of kidney tubules at 200x magnification (the source gives a cross section). The tubules are lined by cube-shaped cells with round nuclei, and a few lumens contain fine granular debris. Compare the lining cells with the small nuclei of the surrounding tissue.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Kidney tubules with interstitial cells between them
images.description: H&E-stained section of kidney tubules at 200x magnification (the source gives a cross section). Tubules with pale lumens are separated by tissue containing many small, dark nuclei. The lining cells have round nuclei and a cube-like shape.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Kidney tubules at high power: cuboidal cells with round nuclei
images.description: H&E-stained section of kidney tubules at 400x magnification (the source gives a cross section). The lining cells are cube-shaped with round, central nuclei, and the tubule lumens are clear. Use it to see the outlines of individual lining cells.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Kidney tubules set in dense cellular tissue
images.description: H&E-stained section of kidney tubules at 200x magnification (the source gives a cross section). The tubules have pale lumens lined by cuboidal cells with round nuclei, and they run through tissue packed with small cells. Look for the difference between the lining cells and the cells around them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Blurred view of pale tissue through a microscope eyepiece
images.description: A photo taken through a microscope eyepiece, showing a round, blurred and unevenly lit field of pale tissue. Some polygonal cells and round nuclei are just visible, but the stain and cell outlines are unclear. It is too poor to confirm the tissue, so it is marked low quality.
images.author: Iv.tena.ok

tissues.name: Simple columnar epithelium
tissues.summary: A single layer of tall, column-shaped cells with oval nuclei near their bases, lining the stomach, intestines and gallbladder. The cells absorb nutrients or secrete mucus, and a ciliated form lines the uterine tube.
features: Single layer of tall columnar cells with oval nuclei near the base
Brush border of microvilli on the luminal surface of absorptive cells
Goblet cells, pale and mucus-filled, scattered among the columnar cells of the intestine
Goblet cells are absent from the stomach surface
Ciliated form in the uterine tube, with cilia on the luminal surface

images.title: Brush border and goblet cells in simple columnar epithelium of mammalian gut
images.description: Cross section of mammalian gut at 400x, showing a single layer of tall columnar cells with elongated dark nuclei, pale blue-grey goblet cells scattered among them, and blue-stained connective tissue below. The stain is not given in the source; the blue collagen suggests a trichrome-type stain. Students should look for the brush border as a thin fringe along the luminal edge and for the goblet cells.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Goblet cells among tall columnar cells in mammalian gut
images.description: Cross section of mammalian gut at 400x, with tall columnar cells that have dark elongated nuclei and several pale goblet cells whose contents appear pale blue-grey in this stain. Blue-stained connective tissue lies beneath the epithelium; the stain is not given in the source, and the colours suggest a trichrome-type stain. Students should find the goblet cells among the columnar cells and the nuclei at their bases.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Goblet cells in gut epithelium around a curved lumen
images.description: Cross section of mammalian gut at 200x, with the epithelium curving around a pale lumen and pale blue goblet cells among the tall columnar cells near the luminal surface. Loose connective tissue with many small dark nuclei and blue collagen lies below; the stain is not given, and the colours suggest a trichrome-type stain. Students should find the goblet cells near the surface and the connective tissue beneath the epithelium.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Tall columnar cells with elongated dark nuclei in gut mucosa
images.description: Cross section of mammalian gut at 400x, probably stained with H&E (pink cytoplasm, dark purple nuclei; the source gives no stain), showing a sheet of tall columnar cells with elongated nuclei at varying heights. The luminal edge is a fine line along the surface, and loose connective tissue with scattered dark nuclei lies beside the epithelium. Students should count the single layer of columnar cells and find the nuclei and the luminal border.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Simple columnar epithelium with goblet cells, seen by phase contrast
images.description: A 400x phase contrast view of mammalian gut in cross section, with tall columnar cells having brown-red nuclei and pale blue goblet cells on either side of a wide central lumen. It shows the same field as the stained image in this set, so the two can be compared directly. Students should find the goblet cells, the nuclei at the bases of the columnar cells and the luminal edge.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Tall columnar cells with goblet cells on either side of a lumen
images.description: A 400x cross section of mammalian gut stained with an H&E-like stain (pink cytoplasm, dark purple nuclei), showing two sheets of tall columnar cells with a wide pale lumen between them. Pale blue goblet cells sit among the columnar cells, with oval nuclei lying towards the bases of the cells. Students should find the single layer of columnar cells, the basal nuclei and the goblet cells.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Gut folds lined by tall columnar cells, with blue connective tissue beside them
images.description: A 100x cross section of mammalian gut in a trichrome-type stain (the source does not name it; blue connective tissue, dark maroon nuclei), showing several mucosal folds lined by a single layer of tall columnar cells. Pale goblet cells are visible among the columnar cells, and blue connective tissue lies beside the folds on the right. Students should see the folds, the tall cells with dark nuclei and the goblet cells.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Gut mucosal folds with a thick outer muscle layer
images.description: A 40x cross section of mammalian gut, probably trichrome-stained (blue connective tissue, dark nuclei, pink muscle; the source gives no stain), showing several mucosal folds lined by tall columnar cells with dark nuclei. A thick band of pink tissue with elongated nuclei, probably smooth muscle, forms the outer wall on the right. Students should compare the mucosal folds with the wall beneath them and find the goblet cells among the epithelium.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

tissues.name: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium
tissues.summary: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is a single layer of cells whose nuclei sit at different heights, so it looks layered although every cell touches the basement membrane. It lines the nasal cavity, trachea and bronchi, where cilia and goblet-cell mucus carry trapped particles up towards the pharynx.
features: Nuclei at different heights, though every cell touches the basement membrane
Tall columnar cells with a fringe of motile cilia on the free surface
Goblet cells: pale, mucus-filled cells scattered among the ciliated cells
Basal cells: small round nuclei lying against the basement membrane
Lamina propria below, with blood vessels; cartilage and glands in larger airways

images.title: Mammalian trachea wall: epithelium, lamina propria and cartilage
images.description: Light micrograph of a cross section through the mammalian trachea at 100x, as the source states. The source gives no stain; the red epithelium and yellow-green connective tissue look like a trichrome-type stain. The thin ciliated epithelium with goblet cells sits on loose lamina propria, with pale tracheal cartilage at the lower left.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Mammalian trachea: ciliated epithelium, goblet cells and cartilage
images.description: Light micrograph of a cross section through the mammalian trachea at 200x, as the source states. The stain is not stated; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Tall ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells line the airway, with submucosal glands between them and the pale cartilage on the other side, which has scattered chondrocytes.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Mammalian trachea at low power: epithelium, cartilage and glands
images.description: Low-power light micrograph of a cross section through the mammalian trachea at 40x, as the source states. The source gives no stain; the red epithelium and yellow-green connective tissue suggest a trichrome-type stain. The thin epithelium runs along the top, with loose connective tissue beneath it, pale cartilage at the left and clusters of submucosal glands at the lower right.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Mammalian trachea: ciliated epithelium over submucosal glands
images.description: Light micrograph of a cross section through the mammalian trachea at 100x, as the source states. The source gives no stain; the red epithelium and yellow-green stroma suggest a trichrome-type stain. The pseudostratified epithelium with goblet cells sits on fibrous lamina propria, and clusters of submucosal glands lie along the lower edge.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Mammalian trachea: ciliated epithelium, glands and hyaline cartilage
images.description: Light micrograph of a cross section through the mammalian trachea at 200x, as the source states. The source gives no stain; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Tall ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells line the airway on the left, with submucosal glands beside them and hyaline cartilage with scattered chondrocytes in the centre.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium: numbered schematic
images.description: Simple numbered schematic (not a micrograph) of the airway epithelium, with its caption in Czech. The labels identify the basement membrane (1), a goblet cell with mucin granules (2), a ciliated cell (3), a brush cell with microvilli (4), the mucus layer (5) and basal cells (6). Nuclei sit at different heights, so the layer looks stratified although every cell reaches the basement membrane.
images.author: HynekJanac

images.title: Respiratory epithelium with mucus moving towards the pharynx (English labels)
images.description: Coloured medical illustration rather than a micrograph, with a body outline showing the location of the trachea and an enlarged view of the respiratory lining. Mucus with trapped particles moves up towards the pharynx over ciliated columnar cells, goblet cells and stem cells. Labels mark the cilia, mucus layer, lamina propria and basement membrane, and the source gives no stain or magnification.

tissues.name: Stratified squamous epithelium (non-keratinised)
tissues.summary: Stratified squamous epithelium without a keratin layer, so its superficial cells stay nucleated. It lines moist surfaces such as the oral cavity, oesophagus, vagina and anal canal, where many cell layers resist abrasion.
features: Many layers of cells with no keratin layer on the surface
Superficial squamous cells are flattened and still have nuclei
Middle layers of polygonal cells that become taller towards the base
Basal layer of cuboidal stem cells on the basement membrane
Glycogen-rich cells in the vagina appear clear
Lines the oral cavity, oesophagus, vagina, ectocervix and anal canal, and covers the cornea

images.title: Oropharynx mucosa of the soft palate with stratified squamous epithelium
images.description: Eight-panel H&E figure (A to H) of the oropharyngeal mucosa of the soft palate, with the non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium marked se in several panels. Mucous glands lie in the submucosa and some open onto the surface, while connective tissue papillae project into the epithelium. The source gives scale bars of 10, 50 and 100 μm for different panels, so compare magnification by the bars.
images.author: Gunes V, Atalan G, Bayram LC, Varol K, Erol H, et al.

tissues.name: Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinised)
tissues.summary: Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium forms the epidermis of the skin. Basal cells divide and move upwards, flattening into anucleate, keratin-filled squames that are shed from the surface and make the skin waterproof.
features: Stratum basale: a single row of cuboidal to columnar cells on the basement membrane
Stratum spinosum: several layers of polyhedral cells with 'prickle' spines from desmosomes
Stratum granulosum: a few layers of cells packed with basophilic keratohyalin granules
Stratum lucidum: a pale, clear band seen only in thick skin (palms and soles)
Stratum corneum: a thick top layer of flattened, anucleate, keratin-filled squames

tissues.name: Transitional epithelium (urothelium)
tissues.summary: Transitional epithelium, or urothelium, is a stretchable stratified epithelium that lines the urinary tract from the renal calyces to the proximal urethra. Its surface umbrella cells form a barrier that stops urine leaking into the wall, and the layers thin as the organ fills.
features: Large dome-shaped umbrella cells on the luminal surface, some binucleate
About 6–7 cell layers when relaxed, flattening to 2–3 layers when distended
Pear-shaped intermediate cells in the middle layers
Small cuboidal basal cells resting on the lamina propria
Mucosal folds in a contracted specimen that flatten out when the organ is distended

images.title: Urothelium lining mucosal folds, low power
images.description: Low-power view of urothelium lining several mucosal folds, with blue-staining connective tissue beneath and adipose tissue at the bottom of the field. The circular field suggests a camera photo taken through a microscope eyepiece; the stain is not stated, but the blue collagen and red-pink epithelium suggest a trichrome-type stain, and no magnification is given. Students should trace the folded lining and the thin epithelium on each fold, as individual cells are not resolved at this power.
images.author: Beich15

images.title: Urinary bladder urothelium, H&E stain
images.description: Section through the wall of the urinary bladder showing urothelium with individual cells clearly resolved and the lumen at the top. Large umbrella cells line the surface above several rows of intermediate cells, and smaller basal cells sit on the pink collagen of the lamina propria below. Magnification is not given; students should find the large surface cells with rounded bulges and the fibroblast nuclei in the lamina propria.
images.author: User:Polarlys

tissues.name: Stratified cuboidal & columnar epithelium
tissues.summary: Stratified cuboidal and stratified columnar epithelia are uncommon linings made of two or more layers of cells, found mainly in the ducts of larger glands such as sweat glands and large salivary ducts. Their multiple layers make them mainly protective, and they often form transitional zones between other epithelia.
features: Two or more layers of cells, with only the basal layer resting on the basement membrane
Stratified cuboidal type: roughly cube-shaped surface cells in the ducts of sweat glands
Stratified columnar type: tall columnar surface cells above smaller basal cells
Duct lumen lined by several layers of cells, with connective tissue around the duct
Columnar type found in large salivary ducts, conjunctiva and parts of the male urethra
Transitional zones where another epithelium changes into this one

tissues.name: Pleura & peritoneum (serous membranes)
tissues.summary: Serosa is a serous membrane: a single layer of flat mesothelial cells resting on a thin layer of loose connective tissue, lining body cavities such as the pleura and peritoneum and covering the organs inside them. It secretes a thin serous fluid that lets organs glide smoothly against each other and against the cavity walls.
features: Single layer of flat (simple squamous) mesothelial cells on the free surface
Flattened, oval nuclei that bulge slightly above the cell surface
Thin layer of loose areolar connective tissue directly beneath the mesothelium
Parietal layer lying on skeletal muscle or fat, with blood vessels in the loose tissue
Milky spots (clusters of lymphocytes and macrophages) in the omentum

images.title: Cutaway diagram of the gut wall layers, serosa labelled
images.description: Labelled cutaway diagram of the alimentary canal showing its four wall layers: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and serosa. The serosa is the outermost layer, labelled as areolar connective tissue with an epithelial surface, and it lies next to the mesentery. It is a teaching drawing, so it shows where the serosa sits in the gut wall rather than cell detail.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Parietal peritoneum beneath fascia over muscle, Masson trichrome
images.description: Masson trichrome-stained section showing skeletal muscle at top left, with deep fascia, parietal peritoneum and a blood vessel marked with arrows and labels. The source notes that the stain separates the parietal peritoneum, deep fascia and muscle clearly, but the primo vessel marked PV is not clearly recognisable. Look for the blue collagen of the fascia and peritoneum against the red muscle and fat.
images.author: HyunSuk Jang , Joohwan Yoon , HyunJi Gil , Sharon Jiyoon Jung , Min-Suk Kim , Jin-Kyu Lee , Young-Jae Kim , Kwang-Sup Soh

tissues.name: Loose (areolar) connective tissue
tissues.summary: Loose (areolar) connective tissue is a cell-rich connective tissue with thin, loosely arranged collagen and elastic fibres in abundant hydrated ground substance. It forms the lamina propria under epithelia and surrounds vessels and nerves, and it is the site of oedema and of the early inflammatory response.
features: Fibroblasts, the most common cells, with oval or spindle-shaped nuclei
Thin collagen fibres forming a loose mesh rather than dense bundles
Fine, wavy elastic fibres, thinner than the collagen fibres
Pale ground substance filling the spaces between the fibres
Macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells and leukocytes scattered among the fibroblasts
Lamina propria under epithelia and around vessels and nerves

images.title: Loose areolar connective tissue: tissue spread at 40x
images.description: The source gives 40x for this tissue spread and no stain; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Many small dark nuclei are scattered through a pink fibrous network, with pale open spaces between the fibres. It is a good low-power view for finding the nuclei and the loose, criss-crossing fibres.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Loose areolar connective tissue: tissue spread at 100x, spindle nuclei
images.description: The source gives 100x for this tissue spread and no stain; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Elongated, spindle-shaped nuclei lie among pink collagen fibres, with thin dark wavy fibres crossing the field. It is a useful view for recognising fibroblast nuclei and the fine wavy fibres that are probably elastic.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Loose areolar connective tissue: tissue spread at 200x
images.description: The source gives 200x for this tissue spread and no stain; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Dark elongated nuclei and some rounded nuclei lie in a pink fibrous matrix, with thin dark wavy fibres running across the field. It shows the cell-rich character of the tissue well.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Loose areolar connective tissue: tissue spread at 100x, many nuclei
images.description: The source gives 100x for this tissue spread and no stain; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Numerous dark oval and elongated nuclei are scattered through a pink fibrous network, with fine dark wavy fibres between them. It shows how cell-rich loose connective tissue can be.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Loose areolar connective tissue: tissue spread at 200x, wavy fibres
images.description: The source gives 200x for this tissue spread and no stain; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Dark nuclei sit among pink fibrous bands and pale areas, and thin dark wavy fibres cross the field between them. Use it to tell the wavy fibres apart from the broader pink collagen bands.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Loose areolar connective tissue: tissue spread at 400x, wavy fibres
images.description: The source gives 400x for this tissue spread and no stain; the pink and purple colouring suggests H&E. Dark, wavy threads loop across a pink background, with a few dark nuclei, some near the edges of the field. The threads are probably elastic fibres, though some may be fibre artefacts from spreading the tissue.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Cultured mast cells stained with toluidine blue
images.description: Light micrograph of cultured mast cells at 100x magnification under oil immersion, stained with toluidine blue (Tol Blue in the source). The blue nuclei sit in cells with purple granular cytoplasm, and the source notes the cells may be slightly degranulated after artificial antigen activation. It is not eye tissue and belongs with loose connective tissue, where mast cells normally live.
images.author: Kauczuk

tissues.name: Dense regular connective tissue
tissues.summary: Dense regular connective tissue is made of parallel bundles of type I collagen, which give great tensile strength in one direction. It forms tendons, ligaments and aponeuroses, with fibroblasts (tenocytes in tendon) lying in rows between the bundles.
features: Parallel collagen bundles that all run in one direction
Wavy (crimped) collagen that straightens under load
Rows of flattened fibroblast (tenocyte) nuclei squeezed between the bundles
Few cells overall, so the tissue looks almost uniformly pink in H&E
Looser connective tissue (epitenon) at the margins

images.title: Tendon hierarchy diagram: collagen, fibril, fibre, fascicle and tendon
images.description: Labelled diagram, not a micrograph, so there is no stain or magnification. It shows the levels of tendon structure from collagen up through fibrils, fibres and fascicles to the whole tendon, with the smaller units drawn in cross-section inside each larger one. Students should use it to see how the small units build up the tendon they meet under the microscope.
images.author: Blumpkin999

tissues.name: Dense irregular connective tissue
tissues.summary: Dense irregular connective tissue is made mainly of thick collagen fibre bundles that run in many directions, so it resists stress applied from any side. It forms the reticular dermis of the skin and the capsules of organs, periosteum, perichondrium and dura mater, and it has relatively few cells.
features: Thick collagen bundles interlacing in many directions, not in parallel layers
Few cells: small, spindle-shaped fibroblast nuclei scattered between the bundles
Elastic fibres, where stained, forming a fine dark network among the collagen
Found in the reticular dermis of skin and in organ capsules, periosteum, perichondrium and dura mater
Contrast with dense regular tissue, where the bundles run parallel in one direction

images.title: Dense irregular connective tissue in deep dermis: skin cutaway diagram
images.description: Coloured 3D cutaway diagram of skin showing hair follicles, blood vessels and subcutaneous fat, with a small box marking the sampled area in the deep dermis. The magnified inset shows collagen fibre bundles interlacing in many directions, the dense irregular pattern a student should recognise. It is a teaching diagram rather than a micrograph, so it has no stain or magnification.
images.author: BruceBlaus

tissues.name: Adipose tissue
tissues.summary: Adipose tissue is loose connective tissue specialised for storing energy as fat in adipocytes, and it also secretes hormones such as leptin and adiponectin. White fat holds one large lipid droplet per cell, while brown fat has many small droplets and heat-producing mitochondria.
features: Unilocular white adipocytes: one large lipid droplet pushes the nucleus to the rim (signet-ring appearance)
Lipid is dissolved during processing, so the cells look pale and empty
Thin connective tissue septa with small nuclei divide the fat into lobules
Brown fat: many small lipid droplets and many mitochondria, mainly in neonates
Rich capillary network running between the adipocytes

images.title: Adipose tissue schematic beside H&E micrograph
images.description: Anatomy and Physiology teaching figure from the Connexions website: on the left a schematic of rounded adipocytes separated by pink connective tissue, on the right an H&E micrograph of adipose tissue with matching labels. No magnification is given. Students should match the stored lipid in each schematic cell with the empty-looking cells in the micrograph, and find the flattened nucleus at one edge of a cell.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Adipose tissue at 200x with a blood vessel at lower left
images.description: Cross section of adipose tissue at 200x as given in the source, stained pink and purple, probably H&E (the source does not name the stain). Large white adipocytes are packed together and separated by thin septa with small dark nuclei. A dark-staining blood vessel at the lower left gives a useful landmark against the fat cells.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Adipose tissue at 400x: cropped view of unilocular fat cells
images.description: Cropped version of the 41066513194 photograph, a cross section of adipose tissue at 400x as given in the source. It shows the same unilocular adipocytes and thin septa with dark nuclei at some junctions, so it repeats the uncropped image.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Adipose tissue at 400x: unilocular fat cells and thin septa
images.description: Cross section of adipose tissue at 400x as given in the source, with a pink stain, probably H&E. Polygonal unilocular adipocytes are separated by thin pink septa, and dark nuclei sit at some septal junctions. Students should find the empty-looking fat cells and the septal nuclei between them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Adipose tissue at 400x with a dark structure at the left edge
images.description: Cross section of adipose tissue at 400x as given in the source, with a pink and purple stain, probably H&E. Unilocular fat cells are separated by thin septa with dark nuclei at several junctions, and a dark-staining structure runs down the left edge. Students should note the contrast between the fat cells and the denser stained strand at the edge.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Adipose tissue at 400x with a thick purple fibrous septum
images.description: Cross section of adipose tissue at 400x as given in the source, probably H&E. Most unilocular adipocytes are separated by thin septa, but a thicker purple fibrous strand runs across the top centre of the field. Students should compare this thicker septum with the thin walls between most of the fat cells.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Adipose tissue at 100x with a blue collagen band (trichrome)
images.description: Low-power cross section of adipose tissue at 100x as given in the source, appearing to be a trichrome stain with collagen in blue. Small white adipocytes fill most of the field, and a dense blue band of collagen runs along the lower edge. Students should notice the probable vessels scattered through the fat, shown as dark round profiles.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

tissues.name: Reticular connective tissue
tissues.summary: Reticular connective tissue is a fine, branching meshwork of type III collagen fibres made by reticular cells (specialised fibroblasts). It forms the supporting framework of lymphoid and haematopoietic organs such as lymph nodes, spleen and bone marrow.
features: Fine, branching reticular fibres forming a delicate three-dimensional mesh
Fibres are argyrophilic: they turn black with silver stains and are faint in H&E
Reticular cells (fibroblast-like, with long processes) lying along the fibres
Mesh filled with lymphocytes or blood-forming cells in lymph node, spleen and bone marrow
Fibres wrap around blood vessels and sinuses within the organ

images.title: Reticular fibres: diagram beside a silver-stained lymphoid tissue micrograph
images.description: Left: a schematic of reticular connective tissue, with blue-green reticular fibres forming a mesh and small yellow nuclei lying among them. Right: a silver-stained micrograph of lymphoid tissue, where the reticular fibres appear as black strands among purple-stained cells. Students should match the schematic fibre mesh to the black fibres seen under silver staining.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Lymphoid organ at low power: round nodules divided by reticular fibres
images.description: Cross section of a lymphoid organ at 40x; the source does not name the organ, but it is likely a lymph node or spleen. It appears to be silver-stained, with black fibres on a pink-purple background. The round nodules are separated by dark bands of reticular fibres, showing how the fibre framework divides the organ into compartments.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Lymphoid tissue at 100x: dense lymphocytes beside a fine reticular mesh
images.description: Cross section of lymphoid tissue at 100x, with a silver-type stain (black fibres on a pink background). Densely packed dark lymphocytes fill the upper left, while the rest of the field shows a fine black mesh of reticular fibres around paler cells. Students should see the mesh as the framework that holds the cells in place.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Reticular fibres at 100x: a thick fibre band and a pale lumen
images.description: Cross section at 100x, silver-stained, with a pale rounded lumen near the top centre. A thick dark fibre band crosses the lower centre and contrasts with the fine black mesh of reticular fibres spreading through the pink-stained cells. Dense lymphoid cells fill the lower right.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Reticular fibre mesh with dense lymphoid cells at 200x
images.description: Cross section at 200x, silver-stained, with black reticular fibres forming a mesh around pink-stained cells. A dense cluster of dark lymphoid nuclei sits in the upper left, and a single dark fibre runs vertically near the top centre. Students should trace the thin, branching fibres that link neighbouring cells.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Fine reticular fibre network among pink cells at 200x
images.description: Cross section at 200x, silver-stained, showing a fine network of black, branching reticular fibres winding between pink-stained cells. Dark lymphoid nuclei form a dense cluster on the left side. Students should follow the thin fibres from cell to cell to see how the mesh is built.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Reticular fibres outlining a rounded structure at 400x
images.description: Cross section at 400x, silver-stained, with thick black reticular fibres outlining a rounded grey structure near the centre. Finer fibres spread out from it through pink cells with round nuclei. Students should notice how the fibres follow the outlines of the cells and wrap around the central structure.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Reticular fibre network among cells at 400x
images.description: Cross section at 400x, silver-stained, with black reticular fibres forming a branching mesh around many pink-stained cells with round purple nuclei. This is one of the two highest-power views in the set, so it shows the fibres as thin strands running between the cells. A thicker fibre runs along the top right edge.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

tissues.name: Hyaline cartilage
tissues.summary: Hyaline cartilage is the most common type of cartilage, a glassy, avascular tissue whose matrix is rich in type II collagen and aggrecan. It covers articular surfaces, forms the costal cartilages and airway rings, and acts as the template for long-bone growth at the growth plate.
features: Glassy, homogeneous matrix with no visible collagen fibres in routine H&E sections
Chondrocytes sit in lacunae, often in isogenous groups
Basophilic territorial matrix around each cell group, rich in aggrecan
Perichondrium: dense fibrous sheath with flattened cells, present except on articular surfaces
Avascular: no blood vessels in the matrix, so nutrients diffuse through it

images.title: Hyaline cartilage under polarised light: lacunae and chondrocytes
images.description: Hyaline cartilage viewed under polarised light, with a scale bar of 50 micrometres; no magnification is given. The source gives the stain as haematoxylin and eosin. Lacunae show as pale ovals, many holding a dark chondrocyte nucleus, against a yellow-brown matrix.
images.author: Emmanuelm at en.wikipedia

images.title: Hyaline cartilage section with scattered chondrocytes in lacunae
images.description: Microscope section of hyaline cartilage; the source gives no stain or magnification. The matrix is uniformly pink, with scattered oval lacunae, each holding a chondrocyte with a dark nucleus and often a pale shrinkage halo.
images.author: Nbnidhi

images.title: Articular cartilage zones: superficial, middle and deep
images.description: Three stacked micrographs of articular cartilage, labelled A (superficial zone), D (middle zone) and G (deep zone), each with a scale bar; no magnification is given. The stain appears to be haematoxylin and eosin, with a pink matrix and purple nuclei. The superficial zone has small, densely packed cells, the middle zone has rounder cells scattered through the matrix, and the deep zone has cells arranged in vertical columns.
images.author: Catherine A. Bautista, Hee Jun Park, Courtney M. Mazur, Roy K. Aaron, Bahar Bilgen

images.title: Deep zone of articular cartilage: chondrocytes in vertical columns
images.description: Micrograph of the deep zone of articular cartilage with a scale bar; no magnification is given. The stain appears to be haematoxylin and eosin, with a pink matrix and purple nuclei. Chondrocytes sit in lacunae arranged in vertical columns perpendicular to the surface, and the lower left shows the cut edge of the section. It appears to be the same micrograph as the deep zone panel of the three-zone figure.
images.author: Catherine A. Bautista, Hee Jun Park, Courtney M. Mazur, Roy K. Aaron, Bahar Bilgen

images.title: Hyaline, fibro and elastic cartilage compared, with micrographs
images.description: Teaching figure comparing three cartilage types, each with a diagram and a micrograph: hyaline cartilage (a), fibrocartilage (b) and elastic cartilage (c). Only panel (a) concerns this tissue, where the diagram shows chondrocytes in lacunae within a pale matrix and the micrograph shows pink matrix with pale lacunae.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Low-power eyepiece photo of a pink tissue strip
images.description: Phone photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece, showing a pale pink strip of tissue with possible lacunae at low power. The circular field is heavily vignetted and the image is soft, so individual chondrocytes are hard to make out. The source gives no stain or magnification.
images.author: Iv.tena.ok

tissues.name: Elastic cartilage
tissues.summary: Elastic cartilage is a flexible cartilage whose matrix holds a dense network of elastic fibres alongside collagen, so it can bend and then spring back to shape. It forms the auricle of the ear, the epiglottis, the external acoustic meatus and the auditory tube.
features: Dense network of elastic fibres in the matrix, staining dark with orcein or Verhoeff stains
Chondrocytes sitting in lacunae within the matrix
A perichondrium (dense fibrous layer) around the cartilage, as in hyaline cartilage
Found in the auricle of the ear, epiglottis, external acoustic meatus and auditory tube

images.title: Elastic cartilage band in a skin section, at low power
images.description: A cross section at 40x of mammalian elastic cartilage, with a band of cartilage running across the middle of the field. The tissue above and below it looks like skin, with hair follicles and hair shafts. Students should trace the band of lacunae and see how it sits between the skin layers.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Elastic cartilage in cross section, with chondrocytes in lacunae
images.description: A cross section at 200x of mammalian elastic cartilage, showing a band of cartilage with many chondrocytes sitting in pale-rimmed lacunae within a dark-staining matrix. Fibrous connective tissue lies above and below the band. Students should look for the rounded cells in their lacunae and the dark matrix between them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Elastic cartilage band with overlying epithelium and a blood vessel
images.description: A cross section at 100x of mammalian elastic cartilage, with a band of lacunae running across the middle of the field. Pink-purple epithelium lies over the top left, and a small round vessel with a central lumen sits below the cartilage among bundles of fibrous tissue. Students should compare the dark matrix of the band with the paler connective tissue around it.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Elastic cartilage at 400x: rows of lacunae in dark matrix
images.description: A cross section at 400x of mammalian elastic cartilage, with rows of chondrocytes in lacunae separated by dark-staining matrix. Fibrous connective tissue lies above and below the band. Students should note the pale rims and dark cores of the lacunae and compare them with the matrix that fills the gaps.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Elastic cartilage lobules among fat and glands, at low power
images.description: A low-power cross section at 40x of mammalian elastic cartilage, with several dark lobules of cartilage embedded in pale, vacuolated fatty tissue. Grey-stained glandular lobules and a dense fibrous band lie along the bottom of the field. Students should find the cartilage lobules with their lacunae and see how fat separates them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Elastic cartilage island surrounded by fat, at 100x
images.description: A cross section at 100x of mammalian elastic cartilage, showing a rounded island of cartilage with many lacunae in a dark matrix. Pale, vacuolated fatty tissue lies on the left and right, and dense fibrous tissue wraps the island. Students should find the lacunae around the edge of the island and compare them with the dark matrix at its centre.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Elastic cartilage at 200x: chondrocytes in lacunae against dark matrix
images.description: A cross section at 200x of mammalian elastic cartilage, with chondrocytes in bright-rimmed lacunae set against a dark matrix. Pale, loosely fibrous connective tissue lies to the left. Students should compare the cell-filled lacunae with the uniform dark matrix around them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Elastic cartilage at the edge: chondrocytes and perichondrium
images.description: A cross section at 400x of mammalian elastic cartilage, with chondrocytes in lacunae in the upper part and dark matrix above them. The matrix grades into flattened fibrous connective tissue along the bottom, where elongated nuclei lie. Students should compare the rounded cells in lacunae with the elongated, fibroblast-like nuclei of the perichondrium.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

tissues.name: Fibrocartilage
tissues.summary: Fibrocartilage is a tough, transitional form of cartilage in which thick bundles of type I collagen run between rows of fibrochondrocytes. It resists both compression and tension, and is found in the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci and labra.
features: Thick, dense bundles of type I collagen, often wavy and running in parallel
Fibrochondrocytes in rows between the collagen bundles, sitting in small lacunae
No perichondrium: the tissue merges straight into the surrounding dense connective tissue
Gradual transition where a tendon or ligament attaches to bone (enthesis)
Found in the annulus fibrosus of intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, menisci and labra

images.title: Fibrocartilage at low power: thick collagen bundles with scattered cells
images.description: Cross section of fibrocartilage at 40x magnification, stained blue; the stain is not named in the source, but the strong blue collagen suggests a trichrome. Thick, wavy collagen bundles run diagonally across most of the field, with small purple cell nuclei scattered between them and a paler, more cellular zone at the upper right. Students should find the bundles and the cells lying among them, and compare the two zones.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Fibrocartilage at high power: fibrochondrocytes between wavy collagen bundles
images.description: Cross section of fibrocartilage at 400x magnification, with the same blue collagen staining as the lower-power view; the stain is not named in the source. Wavy collagen bundles fill the field, and small oval purple fibrochondrocyte nuclei lie scattered between them, some with a pale halo around the cell. Students should look for these cells sitting between the bundles and for the pale rims around some of them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Fibrocartilage at medium power: collagen bundles beside a cell-rich zone
images.description: Cross section of fibrocartilage at 100x magnification, stained blue; the stain is not named in the source. Dense, wavy collagen bundles fill the left of the field, while the right side is paler and has more scattered cell nuclei. Students should compare the dense bundled area with the paler, cell-rich area and find the nuclei in each.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Fibrocartilage at 200x: fibrochondrocytes among collagen bundles
images.description: Cross section of fibrocartilage at 200x magnification, stained blue with purple cell nuclei; the stain is not named in the source. Oval nuclei are spread through the wavy collagen, and a few cells are surrounded by a pale halo. Students should find the cell nuclei and see how they are spaced along the bundles.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Fibrocartilage at high power: cell nuclei in wavy collagen
images.description: Cross section of fibrocartilage at 400x magnification, stained blue; the stain is not named in the source. Reddish-purple fibrochondrocyte nuclei lie within wavy collagen bundles, and several cells have pale rims. Students should identify the nuclei and the dense, wavy collagen that surrounds them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Mammal fibrocartilage: photo of a red and blue stained section
images.description: Photograph of a stained mammal fibrocartilage section taken through a microscope, so the field is circular with dark edges; the source gives no magnification and does not name the stain. A dense red band runs across the top, a paler band lies below it, and a blue area with scattered pink-red rounded structures fills the lower left. The source says collagen and elastic fibres are shown, but they are not clearly separable in this photo, so students should compare the red band with the blue area.
images.author: Magda Yurchishin

images.title: Human meniscal cells in culture: spindle-shaped cells with long processes
images.description: Hoffman modulation contrast image of cultured human meniscus cells, so this shows a cell culture rather than a tissue section. The cells are spindle-shaped with long processes extending from the cell body, as seen in low-confluence monolayer culture, and the scale bar is 10 micrometres. Students can use the scale bar to judge cell size, but should not expect to see the matrix of the intact tissue here.
images.author: Helen E Gruber, David Mauerhan, Yin Chow, Jane A Ingram, H James Norton, Edward N Hanley and Yubo Sun

images.title: White fibrocartilage of an intervertebral disc: drawing of wavy fibres and cells
images.description: Line drawing of white fibrocartilage from an intervertebral disc, showing wavy, parallel fibre bundles with oval cells lying in lacunae, many in pairs or small groups. As a drawing it has no stain or magnification, and it shows the cell and fibre pattern more clearly than a slide would. Students should find the cells in their lacunae and the wavy fibres around them.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Compact (cortical) bone
tissues.summary: Compact (cortical) bone is the dense outer layer of bone, built from osteons whose concentric lamellae wrap around a central canal carrying blood vessels and nerves. It gives bone its strength and stiffness, with osteocytes sitting in lacunae linked by canaliculi.
features: Concentric lamellae wrapped around a central (Haversian) canal holding vessels and nerves
Osteocytes sitting in lacunae, linked by canaliculi
Perforating (Volkmann) canals running across the osteons to join central canals
Circumferential and interstitial lamellae filling the gaps between osteons
Outer surface covered by periosteum, with Sharpey fibres entering the bone

images.title: Compact bone: ground section at 40x showing several osteons
images.description: Cross-section of ground human bone at 40x magnification, showing many osteons packed together, each with a dark central canal. The section appears unstained, with the canals shown as black holes in a pale tan matrix. Use it to see the overall arrangement of osteons and their Haversian canals before moving to higher power.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Unclear polarised-light view of possible bone tissue
images.description: Tall close-up that appears to be a microscope view with colour fringes, showing parallel striated bands on the left and rounded, stippled profiles on the right. The source caption is a generic description of laboratory work, with no magnification or stain given. The tissue cannot be confidently identified as compact bone, so the image is not a good teaching example.
images.author: Iv.tena.ok

tissues.name: Spongy (cancellous) bone
tissues.summary: Spongy (cancellous) bone is a porous lattice of trabeculae, thin bony plates and rods, with marrow filling the spaces between them; it forms the interior of the epiphyses, vertebral bodies and flat bones. Its trabeculae are aligned along the lines of mechanical stress, giving strength for low weight and a large surface for bone remodelling.
features: Trabeculae of lamellar bone with no osteons, so no central canals
Osteocytes in lacunae within the trabeculae, linked by canaliculi
Cuboidal osteoblasts lining surfaces where new bone is being laid down
Multinucleated osteoclasts in Howship lacunae on resorbing surfaces
Marrow spaces between trabeculae, holding fat and haematopoietic cells

images.title: Spongy bone diagram: trabeculae, lamellae and bone cells
images.description: Labelled textbook diagram from an Anatomy and Physiology illustration (Connexions), with the same layout as the Spanish-labelled version: the upper femur, a boxed view of the trabecular lattice, and an enlarged trabecula showing lamellae, lacunae, osteocytes, osteoclasts and osteoblasts. It is a schematic with no stain or magnification, and it is useful for seeing how trabeculae are built from layers of lamellae and how bone cells sit on the surface.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Compact and spongy bone: cut-away diagram with osteons and trabeculae
images.description: Coloured cut-away diagram of bone with Hebrew labels, translated here, showing compact bone with osteons and Haversian and Volkmann's canals alongside trabeculae of spongy bone, with blood vessels. It is a schematic rather than a microscope image, so no stain or magnification applies. Students should compare the dense, osteon-based compact bone with the open trabecular network of spongy bone.
images.author: Ori~

tissues.name: Bone development & growth plate
tissues.summary: Bone forms in two ways: intramembranous ossification lays down bone directly within mesenchyme, while endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model. The epiphyseal growth plate is the cartilage zone that drives longitudinal growth of long bones.
features: Growth plate zones in order: resting, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcified, then bone
Proliferative zone: flattened chondrocytes stacked in neat columns
Hypertrophic zone: enlarged chondrocytes in lacunae, with thin calcified septa between columns
Intramembranous bone: trabeculae forming directly in vascular mesenchyme, with no cartilage model
Osteoblasts lining new bone, osteocytes in lacunae, osteoclasts in resorption pits

images.title: Intramembranous ossification: labelled diagram in four panels
images.description: Labelled teaching diagram from Anatomy and Physiology (Connexions), with panels a to d. Panels a and b show mesenchymal cells becoming osteoblasts, with osteoid and osteocytes forming at an ossification centre. Panels c and d show trabeculae, blood vessels and the fibrous periosteum giving rise to compact and spongy bone, so students should follow the sequence from mesenchyme to bone.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Pubic symphysis: cartilage and bone in one section
images.description: Section of the pubic symphysis, a fibrocartilaginous joint, in pink and purple tones that are probably H&E (the source does not name the stain or give a magnification). Columns of chondrocytes in lacunae sit beside pink bone matrix, and the source notes that the ossification process can be seen. Students should find the cartilage and the bone and see where they meet.
images.author: Luxs96

images.title: Cartilage cell rows giving way to calcified matrix and bone (labelled diagram)
images.description: Historical line drawing, probably from Gray's Anatomy (the file is named Gray293), with no caption in the source. It shows a vertical section of cartilage labelled from the surface down: superficial flattened cells, vertical rows of cells, calcified matrix and bone. Students should see how cartilage cells line up in columns before the matrix calcifies and bone replaces it.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Bone marrow
tissues.summary: Bone marrow is the soft tissue filling bone cavities, where haematopoietic stem cells produce red blood cells, platelets and white blood cells. Red marrow carries out this blood formation, while yellow marrow is mainly fat.
features: Cords of developing blood cells lying between wide, thin-walled sinusoids
Megakaryocytes: the largest marrow cells, with lobed nuclei, releasing platelets into the sinusoids
Erythroblastic islands: erythroid precursors with round nuclei clustered around a central macrophage
Granulocyte precursors with granular cytoplasm, such as eosinophil myelocytes with orange-red granules
Clear fat cells (adipocytes), which increase with age as red marrow turns yellow

images.title: Bone marrow cells: labelled megakaryocyte, eosinophil myelocyte and erythroblast
images.description: Bone marrow aspirate with arrows labelling a megakaryocyte, an eosinophil myelocyte and an orthochromatic erythroblast. The source gives no stain or magnification; it appears to be an H&E-type stain, with pink cytoplasm and dark purple nuclei. Students should compare the large megakaryocyte, with its lobed nucleus, against the much smaller round-nucleated erythroid and granulocyte precursors around it.

images.description: Unlabelled bone marrow aspirate field with a megakaryocyte near the centre, recognisable by its large size and lobed dark nucleus, and granular eosinophil myelocytes with orange-red cytoplasm. The source gives no stain or magnification; it appears to be an H&E-type stain. images.title: Cut bone end showing red and yellow marrow, with scale bar
images.description: Gross photograph of a cut bone end, not microscopy, with a scale bar at the top left. Red marrow lies around the edge and yellow marrow in the centre. It is the same specimen photograph as the labelled 619 Red and Yellow Bone Marrow image.
images.author: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology

images.title: Haematopoietic lineage tree from stem cell to blood cells and macrophages
images.description: Schematic lineage diagram, not a micrograph, tracing haematopoiesis from a multipotent haematopoietic stem cell through myeloid and lymphoid stem cells. Megakaryoblasts give megakaryocytes and platelets, proerythroblasts give erythrocytes, myeloblasts give basophils, neutrophils and eosinophils, and monoblasts give monocytes and macrophages. No stain applies; use it to trace each mature cell back to its progenitor.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Cut bone end with labelled red and yellow marrow
images.description: Gross photograph of a cut bone end, not microscopy, with labels for the outer surface of the bone, red marrow and yellow marrow. It is a teaching figure showing where red marrow lies in the bone, and it is the labelled version of the 2205 Bone Marrow photograph.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Osteoclast formation from haematopoietic precursors, marrow to bone surface
images.description: Schematic, not a micrograph, showing mononuclear precursors from haematopoietic stem cells in the marrow and blood vessels differentiating into osteoclasts on the bone surface. The enlarged inset shows an osteoclast with a ruffled border and sealing zone, with enzymes such as cathepsin K (CTSK), MMP9 and TRAP. No stain applies; its focus is osteoclast biology, so it links marrow to bone more than it shows the marrow itself.
images.author: Sharon Russo

images.title: Haematopoietic stem cell migration from embryo to fetal liver and bone marrow
images.description: Schematic, not a micrograph, showing haematopoietic sites in the embryo, yolk sac and placenta, with stem cells moving to the fetal liver and then to the bone marrow of a long bone. Homing signals listed beside the marrow include CXCL12/CXCR4 and c-kit/SCF. No stain applies, and the figure is mainly about embryonic and fetal haematopoiesis rather than adult marrow.
images.author: Magnon, C. and Frenette, P.S., Hematopoietic stem cell trafficking (July 14, 2008), StemBook, ed. The Stem Cell Research Community, StemBook, doi/10.3824/stembook.1.8.1, http://www.stembook.org.

tissues.name: Blood cells
tissues.summary: Blood is a fluid connective tissue in which erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets are suspended in plasma. In a stained smear the erythrocytes are by far the most numerous cells, with white cells and platelets scattered among them.
features: Erythrocytes: anucleate biconcave discs, about 7.5 µm, the most numerous cells and a size reference
Neutrophils (40–70% of white cells): multilobed nucleus with fine granules
Lymphocytes (20–40%): round, dense nucleus with a thin rim of cytoplasm
Monocytes: large cell with a kidney-shaped nucleus; they become macrophages in tissue
Eosinophils: bilobed nucleus with red granules; basophils: dark purple granules
Platelets: small anucleate fragments, 2–3 µm across

images.title: Normal human blood smear at low magnification
images.description: Low-power view of a normal human peripheral blood smear with a 100 µm scale bar; the source does not state the stain. The field is packed with erythrocytes, so white cells and platelets show only as occasional dark specks at this magnification. Students should use it to see how densely red cells fill the blood and how uniform they are.
images.author: Степанюк Ярослав|Борис Максим

images.title: Spherocyte beside a normal red blood cell in scanning electron microscopy
images.description: Unstained scanning electron micrograph of two red cells side by side: on the left a spherocyte, a rounded cell without the central pallor of a normal cell, and on the right a normal biconcave red cell. Students should compare the rounded outline of the spherocyte with the dished profile of the normal cell.
images.author: Joan-Lluis Vives-Corrons, Elena Krishnevskaya

images.title: Normal and lipid-laden white blood cells, with tissue panels
images.description: Six-panel figure on lipid inclusions in white cells. A and B look Romanowsky-stained; per the source, A is a normal white cell and B a white cell filled with lipid droplets, with arrows marking inclusions in B. C is a fluorescence image of two nuclei with green spots arrowed, and D to F are tissue sections (a brown-stained section, an electron micrograph and a pink section full of clear vacuoles); students should compare the clear inclusions in B with the normal cell in A.
images.author: Missaglia S, Coleman RA, Mordente A, and Tavian D.

images.title: B lymphocyte in colourised scanning electron microscopy
images.description: Colourised scanning electron micrograph of a B cell from a human donor (NIAID credit); the colour is added to the image, so no stain applies. The round cell has a rough, folded surface covered in small projections, and the image shows only the outer surface, not the nucleus. Magnification is not given.
images.author: NIAID

images.title: Neutrophil engulfing anthrax bacteria, colourised scanning electron micrograph
images.description: Colourised scanning electron micrograph of a neutrophil (yellow) engulfing anthrax bacteria (orange, rod-shaped), taken with a Leo 1550 scanning electron microscope. The scale bar is 5 µm. Students should see the cell's extensions reaching around the bacteria.
images.author: Volker Brinkmann

images.title: T lymphocyte in colourised scanning electron microscopy
images.description: Colourised scanning electron micrograph of a T lymphocyte (NIAID credit) in teal on a dark background. The round cell has a rough surface covered in short folds and projections, and the colour is added to the image. Magnification is not given, and only the outer surface of the cell is visible.
images.author: NIAID

images.title: Normal red blood cells flowing in a blood vessel, with a cross-section inset
images.description: Medical illustration (not a microscope image, no stain) of normal red blood cells flowing freely through a blood vessel, with an inset showing a cross-section of a normal red cell containing normal haemoglobin. It is about blood cells rather than the capillary wall, so it belongs under the blood tissue.
images.author: NHLBI

tissues.name: Skeletal muscle
tissues.summary: Skeletal muscle is made of long, multinucleated, cross-striated fibres under voluntary control, which contract to move the skeleton. Each fibre forms by fusion of precursor cells, so its nuclei sit at the edge, just beneath the sarcolemma.
features: Oval nuclei pushed to the edge of each fibre; central nuclei suggest pathology or regeneration
Cross-striations: dark A bands, light I bands and Z lines form the sarcomeres, seen at high power
Connective tissue sheaths: endomysium around each fibre, perimysium around fascicles, epimysium around the whole muscle
Satellite cells lie beneath the basal lamina and allow limited regeneration
Type I (slow, oxidative) and type II (fast, glycolytic) fibres intermix within the muscle

images.title: Striated muscle fibre bundles seen through a microscope eyepiece
images.description: Photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece, showing bundles of long, thin, tapering fibres in blue-purple against a pale background. The source gives only the word 'Tissue', with no stain or magnification. Nuclei and cross-striations cannot be resolved, so students cannot use it to find muscle features.
images.author: Naz Amann

images.title: Skeletal muscle T-tubules and sarcoplasmic reticulum (diagram)
images.description: Labelled diagram, not microscopy, of skeletal muscle showing the sarcolemma, the sarcoplasmic reticulum with its terminal cisternae, a T-tubule and the triad. The labels are in Arabic, and the source describes the T-tubule structure and its relationship to the sarcoplasmic reticulum. It is a correct teaching diagram of this tissue, and it is the same figure as the English-labelled image in this set.
images.author:
OpenStax

Derivative: علاء

images.title: Skeletal muscle in longitudinal section with one fibre highlighted
images.description: Longitudinal section of skeletal muscle, with one fibre coloured red and labelled 'Muscle cell (highlighted)', and arrows pointing to nuclei within it. The source gives no stain or magnification, but the pink cytoplasm and dark blue nuclei suggest H&E. Students should see the long, parallel fibres across the field, with the dark nuclei scattered along them.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Skeletal muscle fibre diagram: sarcolemma, myofibrils and striations
images.description: Labelled diagram, not microscopy, of a striated muscle fibre, with the sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, myofibrils and striations marked, and the fibre length shown below. This is the English-labelled version of the same figure as the Spanish image, so students can use either to learn the same structures. It is a correct teaching diagram of this tissue.
images.author: CNX OpenStax

images.title: Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle compared side by side
images.description: Three micrographs side by side, labelled skeletal muscle on the left, smooth muscle in the centre and cardiac muscle on the right, with scale bars of 25 µm, 25 µm and 10 µm. The stain appears to be H&E, though the source does not name it. At this size the skeletal panel's nuclei and striations are not clearly resolved, so students should use the larger images for detail.
images.author: CNX OpenStax

images.title: Skeletal muscle triad: T-tubule between two terminal cisternae (diagram)
images.description: Labelled diagram, not microscopy, of skeletal muscle showing the sarcolemma, the sarcoplasmic reticulum, the terminal cisternae, a T-tubule and the triad that they form. The labels are in English, and the figure is the same as the Arabic-labelled image in this set. It is a correct teaching diagram, and the source describes the T-tubule structure and its relationship to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
images.author: OpenStax

tissues.name: Cardiac muscle (myocardium)
tissues.summary: Cardiac muscle forms the thick muscular wall of the heart (the myocardium) and contracts rhythmically without conscious control. Its branched, striated fibres are joined end to end by intercalated discs, which let them contract as one coordinated unit.
features: Branched, cross-striated fibres that link end to end in chains
One or two central nuclei per fibre, with a pale zone around each nucleus
Intercalated discs: dark, step-like transverse lines where neighbouring fibres meet
Abundant mitochondria (about a third of cell volume) and a rich capillary network between fibres
Purkinje fibres: large pale conducting cells lying beneath the endocardium

images.title: Labelled diagram of cardiac muscle fibres and intercalated discs
images.description: OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology textbook illustration (published 2016), not a micrograph, so no stain or magnification applies. It shows branched cardiac fibres beside a capillary, with the heart at top left marking where the tissue sits, and an inset enlarging an intercalated disc with desmosomes, gap junctions, myofibrils and a mitochondrion. Students should find the central nucleus, the stepped intercalated discs and the gap junctions.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle compared at the same magnification
images.description: Three-panel comparison from University of Michigan Medical School micrographs (2012), with (a) skeletal, (b) smooth and (c) cardiac muscle, all at LM x1600 as given in the source. The panels appear to be H&E stained (pink cytoplasm, purple nuclei). Students should compare the nuclei: skeletal muscle has elongated nuclei at the fibre edges, smooth muscle has spindle-shaped nuclei, and cardiac muscle in panel (c) has oval nuclei within the fibres.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Cardiac muscle fibres in longitudinal section at high power
images.description: H&E-stained cardiac muscle at LM x1600, as given in the source (University of Michigan Medical School, 2012). Parallel pink fibres run diagonally across the field, several with oval nuclei, and pale spaces lie between them. Students should find the nuclei within the fibres and the pale spaces that separate them.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Cardiac muscle diagrams and a stained micrograph of intercalated discs
images.description: Three-part teaching figure described in the source as an anatomical illustration: (a) a schematic of cardiac fibres with nuclei, mitochondria, intercalated discs and a gap junction, (b) a pink and purple micrograph with intercalated discs labelled, and (c) a schematic of a desmosome, gap junction, A band and I band. No magnification is given. Students should use panel (b) to find the dark, transverse intercalated discs in real tissue.
images.author: OpenStax CNX

tissues.name: Smooth muscle
tissues.summary: Smooth muscle is non-striated muscle made of spindle-shaped cells, each with one central nucleus, that forms the walls of hollow organs, blood vessels and airways, and is also found in the iris. Its involuntary contraction moves contents along the gut and changes the diameter of vessels and airways.
features: Spindle-shaped cells, each with one central, cigar-shaped nucleus
No cross-striations, unlike skeletal and cardiac muscle
Nuclei that corkscrew when the cells contract
Parallel sheets of fibres in the walls of gut, vessels, airways and uterus

images.title: Smooth muscle fibres with autonomic nerves: diagram and micrograph
images.description: A two-part OpenStax textbook figure. Part (a) is a diagram of sheets of smooth muscle fibres from the stomach (left) and the eye (right), with autonomic nerve fibres and nuclei labelled. Part (b) is a light micrograph of parallel, pink fibres with elongated purple nuclei; the stain is not named (probably H&E) and no magnification is given. Students should see the single central nucleus of each fibre and how the fibres lie side by side.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Autonomic nerve varicosities on smooth muscle cells: diagram
images.description: A textbook diagram from OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology showing an autonomic nerve running along sheets of smooth muscle cells, with swellings along it called varicosities. An enlarged view on the left shows one varicosity packed with vesicles containing neurotransmitters. Students should see the spindle-shaped cells with central nuclei and the beaded course of the nerve across them.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Smooth muscle: blurred eyepiece photo of a pink tissue piece
images.description: A blurred phone photograph through a microscope eyepiece, showing a pink piece of tissue on a pale background inside a dark circle. Cell outlines and nuclei cannot be made out, and no stain or magnification is given. It cannot confirm the features of smooth muscle, so it adds little for identification.
images.author: Nbnidhi

tissues.name: Peripheral nerve
tissues.summary: Peripheral nerves are bundles of myelinated and unmyelinated axons, grouped into fascicles and wrapped in three connective-tissue sheaths: epineurium, perineurium and endoneurium. They carry nerve impulses between the central nervous system and the rest of the body.
features: Epineurium: dense connective tissue around the whole nerve, containing fat and blood vessels
Perineurium: flattened cell layers around each fascicle, forming the blood-nerve barrier
Endoneurium: delicate connective tissue between the individual axons inside each fascicle
Myelinated axons: round profiles with pale halos in H&E sections
Blood vessels: lie in the epineurium and beside the fascicles

images.title: Peripheral nerve cross-section: perineurium and endoneurium at higher power
images.description: H&E-stained transverse section of a nerve from an OpenStax anatomy figure, with a small inset showing the whole nerve at low power. The dense perineurium forms the band at the edge of the large fascicle on the right, and the endoneurium fills the spaces among the round myelinated axon profiles inside it. The source gives no magnification.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Nerve trunk schematic and H&E cross-section, with placeholder overlay
images.description: Two-panel OpenStax figure: (a) a schematic of a spinal nerve showing the epineurium, fascicles, perineurium, endoneurium and blood vessels, and (b) an H&E-stained cross-section of a nerve trunk. A large 'FPO' placeholder and a line of text about a markup PDF cover the main fascicle in panel (b), so this copy is unsuitable for students. The source gives no magnification.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Peripheral nerve schematic and H&E cross-section, Basque labels
images.description: The same OpenStax nerve figure with Basque labels, in a wider layout: panel (a) is a spinal nerve schematic and panel (b) an H&E-stained cross-section of a nerve trunk. It shows the epineurium, perineurium and axon fascicles, with the endoneurium and blood vessels labelled in the schematic. The source gives no magnification.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Peripheral nerve schematic and H&E cross-section, English labels
images.description: OpenStax figure with (a) a spinal nerve schematic labelled with epineurium, perineurium, endoneurium, fascicles, axons and blood vessels, and (b) an H&E-stained cross-section of a nerve trunk. In panel (b) the epineurium is the outer connective tissue, the perineurium is the dense sheath around the large central fascicle, and the axon fascicles are the smaller bundles. The source gives no magnification.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Peripheral nerve cross-section diagram with fascicles and blood vessels
images.description: A flat-coloured diagram of a peripheral nerve cut across: an orange outer sheath surrounds several fascicles, each drawn as a group of blue and yellow fibre profiles, with red blood vessels and small yellow ovals in the sheath. It is a simplified illustration rather than a microscope image, and an electrode with a lead is drawn at the left end. It is useful for learning how the fascicles and vessels are arranged.
images.author: DataBase Center for Life Science (DBCLS)

images.title: Pencil sketch of a neuron with dendrites, nucleus, myelin and axon
images.description: Hand-drawn pencil sketch of a neuron, with the dendrites, nucleus, myelin sheath and axon labelled. It is a general cell diagram rather than a view of cerebral cortex, and the myelinated axon points to nerve tissue. The four labelled parts match the components described in the source.
images.author: Mckin555

tissues.name: Sensory & autonomic ganglia
tissues.summary: Ganglia are clusters of nerve cell bodies lying outside the central nervous system. Sensory (dorsal root) ganglia carry signals from the body into the spinal cord, while autonomic ganglia relay signals from the CNS to glands, smooth muscle and the heart.
features: Dorsal root ganglion: large round sensory neurons packed together, each ringed by small satellite cells
Autonomic ganglia: smaller multipolar neurons with eccentric nuclei, set among nerve fibres
A large round nucleus with a prominent nucleolus in each neuron
Nissl substance (granular basophilic cytoplasm) in the neuron cell bodies, clearest with cresyl violet
Bundles of wavy nerve fibres (axons) running into or out of the ganglion, with a connective tissue capsule

images.title: Dorsal root ganglion with labelled sensory cell bodies and axon bundles
images.description: A wide view of a dorsal root (spinal) ganglion in a pink and purple section, with the sensory neuron cell bodies in the rounded central mass and bundles of nerve fibres (axons) to one side. It appears to be H&E stained, and the source gives no magnification. Students should look for the many round neuron profiles packed in the ganglion and the wavy fibre bundles around them.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Earthworm nerve ganglion stained green, with recording pins through it
images.description: A photograph through a microscope of an earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris) nerve ganglion stained green with Alexa Fluor 488 dye, so it shows fluorescence rather than a histology stain. Two metal recording pins pass through the tissue, the source says it was mishandled during imaging, and no magnification is given, so the cell detail is poor.
images.author: Erin Asadourian

images.title: Snail section with digestive organs and nerve ganglia
images.description: Light micrograph of two sections (A and B) through a snail (Zospeum sp.), in blue-stained sections with the stain not named in the source, and 500 µm scale bars. images.description: Histological cross sections (panels A to G) of the mollusc Bathyhedyle boucheti, shown in blue-stained sections with scale bars of 100, 200 and 500 µm; the stain is not named in the source. images.title: Ring-shaped loukoumasomes among neurons in a pelvic ganglion
images.description: Fluorescence and confocal micrographs of loukoumasomes, ring-shaped structures in a whole-mounted pelvic (autonomic) ganglion. Panel B shows neuron cell bodies stained blue (MAP2), with the rings stained green (SDL.3D10) and red dots (gamma-tubulin), while panel C shows loukoumasomes lack pericentrin, unlike centrioles. The source gives no species or magnification, and scale bars are in µm.
