tissues.name: Elastic artery (aorta)
tissues.summary: The elastic artery is a large conducting vessel, such as the aorta and its major branches, whose tunica media is built from many concentric elastic lamellae with smooth muscle between them. Its elastic recoil stores energy during systole and keeps blood moving through diastole.
features: Tunica media of 40-70 wavy, fenestrated elastic lamellae stacked concentrically
Smooth muscle nuclei lying between the elastic lamellae in the media
Verhoeff stain: elastic lamellae dark purple to black against pale interlamellar spaces
Media forms most of the wall thickness, unlike the smooth-muscle-dominated muscular artery
Vasa vasorum: small vessels that supply the outer part of the thick wall

images.title: Elastic, muscular and arteriole walls compared in a labelled diagram
images.description: Textbook diagram of three arterial wall types side by side: an elastic artery (left), a muscular artery (centre) and an arteriole (right), each labelled for tunica externa, tunica media and tunica intima. The elastic artery panel shows a thick media packed with wavy elastic fibres, which is the feature to compare with the smooth muscle of the other two. As a drawing it has no stain or magnification.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Artery wall layers with elastic membranes, in a labelled illustration
images.description: Medical illustration titled The Structure of an Artery Wall, with a whole-vessel cross-section and an enlarged segment of the wall. It labels the tunica externa, tunica media, tunica intima, endothelium, and the external and internal elastic membranes. The media is drawn as smooth muscle, so this shows a general artery wall rather than the elastic lamellae of an elastic artery.

tissues.name: Muscular arteries & arterioles
tissues.summary: Muscular (distributing) arteries carry blood to organs and have a thick media of smooth muscle bounded by distinct internal and external elastic laminae. Their smaller branches, the arterioles, are the main site of peripheral resistance and so help set blood pressure.
features: Wavy internal elastic lamina separating the intima from the media
Thick media of many circular layers of smooth muscle, the bulk of the wall
External elastic lamina at the outer edge of the media
Collagen-rich adventitia outside the external elastic lamina
Arterioles with only 1-2 layers of smooth muscle in the media

images.title: Muscular artery in cross section, trichrome-type stain
images.description: Bright-field photomicrograph of a whole cross section of a human artery, with fat and small neighbouring profiles around it. The source does not name the stain, but the blue collagen in the outer coat and the purple-red media suggest a trichrome stain, and no magnification is given. Students should find the wavy internal elastic lamina under the lining, the thick smooth-muscle media and the blue collagen of the outer coat.
images.author: Lord of Konrad

images.title: Muscular-elastic artery in cross section, haematoxylin and eosin
images.description: Light micrograph of a cross section of an artery of the muscular-elastic type, stained with haematoxylin and eosin at x40 magnification as the source states. The pink wall surrounds a pale lumen, and a dark needle-like artefact crosses the left side of the field. At this power the wall layers cannot be separated, so students should use it to see the ring shape and the relative thickness of wall and lumen.
images.author: Андрюша Романов

images.title: Artery wall: tunica intima, media and externa (diagram)
images.description: Labelled illustration, not microscopy, showing a cross-section of an artery and an enlarged wedge of its wall. The layers shown are the tunica intima, tunica media and tunica externa, with the smooth muscle, the internal and external elastic membranes and the endothelium labelled. The thin endothelial lining is one small part of the wall, so the image belongs with the muscular artery tissue rather than simple squamous epithelium.
images.author:
BruceBlaus. When using this image in external sources it can be cited as:

tissues.name: Veins & venules
tissues.summary: Veins and venules carry blood back to the heart at low pressure, and because they hold much of the body's blood they act as capacitance vessels. Their walls are thin, with a thin media and a thick adventitia, and the larger veins, especially in the limbs, have valves that stop blood flowing backwards.
features: Large, thin-walled lumen, often collapsed in sections, compared with the accompanying artery
Thin media with far less smooth muscle than the accompanying artery
Adventitia (outer coat) is the thickest layer of the wall
Valves: pocket-shaped folds of intima in limb veins that stop backflow
Venules: very thin wall, and the site where leukocytes leave the blood in inflammation

images.title: Large vein, medium vein and venule walls: labelled diagram
images.description: Labelled diagram of the wall of a large vein, a medium-sized vein with a closed valve, and a venule, with English labels. It shows the outer, middle and inner coats, smooth muscle cells in the outer coat, vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum, and the valve in the closed position. This is the English version of the same diagram as the Polish one, so the two overlap.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Vein wall layers: labelled cutaway diagram of a vein
images.description: Small labelled diagram of a curved vein with a cutaway showing the wall in colour-coded layers. It is a diagram, so no stain or magnification applies. Students should find the inner lining layer, the middle layer and the outer layer of the wall.
images.author: Author not recorded on Wikimedia Commons (see source page)

images.title: Central vein of a liver lobule, H&E-type section
images.description: Light micrograph of liver tissue in pink and purple, with the stain appearing to be H&E, showing a central vein near the middle of the field with hepatocyte cords around it. The source describes a digital camera photo taken through a microscope and gives no magnification, and a black pointer enters the field from the top. Students should find the small central vein and note that most of the field is liver cells and the vessel is not sharply resolved.
images.author: Jpogi at English Wikipedia

tissues.name: Capillaries & sinusoids
tissues.summary: Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, a single thin layer of endothelial cells on a basement membrane, where oxygen, nutrients and wastes are exchanged between blood and tissue. Their walls are continuous, fenestrated or sinusoidal (discontinuous) depending on the organ, and pericytes wrap their outer surface to help regulate flow.
features: Thin wall of flat endothelial cells, with nuclei bulging into a narrow lumen
Lumen often just wide enough for one red blood cell
Pericytes: small cells outside the endothelium, within the basement membrane
Fenestrations: pores through the endothelium, seen only on electron microscopy
Sinusoids: wide, irregular channels with gaps between endothelial cells (liver, spleen)
Continuous type: tight junctions seal the endothelium (muscle, CNS)

images.title: Liver sinusoid fenestrations in a transmission electron micrograph
images.description: Transmission electron micrograph with no light stain, of liver sinusoids from a three-week-old wild-type animal, with a top panel and a bottom panel at higher magnification (scale bars 500 nm and 200 nm). The sinusoid lumen (Lu) lies beside hepatocytes (He), with the space of Disse (Di) open between them. Students should find the arrowed fenestrations, small pores in the sinusoidal endothelial cells.

images.title: Capillary bed with its arterioles and venules (schematic, Chinese labels)
images.description: Labelled schematic illustration (not a microscope image) of a capillary bed, with Chinese labels, showing an arteriole feeding capillaries through a metarteriole and precapillary sphincters, which drain into a venule. A thoroughfare channel and an arteriovenous anastomosis give direct routes from arteriole to venule that bypass the capillaries. Students should trace blood flow from the arteriole through the capillaries to the venule.

images.title: Capillary bed with its arterioles and venules (schematic)
images.description: Labelled schematic illustration (not a microscope image) of a capillary bed, showing an arteriole feeding a network of capillaries through a metarteriole and precapillary sphincters, which drains into a venule. A thoroughfare channel and an arteriovenous anastomosis are direct routes from arteriole to venule that bypass the capillaries. images.title: Capillary with a red blood cell in pancreatic tissue, electron micrograph
images.description: Transmission electron micrograph of a capillary in pancreatic tissue, with a red blood cell in the lumen (scale bar 1 µm; electron micrograph, no light stain). Acinar cells lie beside the vessel, and a nerve profile with synaptic vesicles sits next to it, as the source notes. Students should find the thin endothelial lining, which the source describes as fenestrated, and the dark, crescent-shaped red blood cell.

images.title: Capillaries in the cerebellum, luxol fast blue and cresyl violet stain
images.description: Light micrograph of a cross section through the cerebellum at 400x magnification, stained with luxol fast blue and cresyl violet, giving a blue-green background with dark blue nuclei. Capillaries show as pale tubes lined by elongated, dark endothelial nuclei, and round dark nuclei of neurons and glia are scattered through the tissue. Students should find the capillary lumens and the flattened endothelial nuclei along their walls, and the pia mater along the top edge.

images.title: Fenestrated capillary wall: cutaway schematic
images.description: Labelled cutaway schematic (not a microscope image) of a fenestrated capillary, showing the basement membrane on the outside, the endothelium on the inside, and tight junctions between endothelial cells. Round fenestrations (pores) pierce the endothelium across the wall. Students should find these pores, which let fluid and small molecules pass quickly in organs such as the kidney glomerulus and endocrine glands.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Sinusoid fenestrations seen from inside, scanning electron micrograph
images.description: Scanning electron micrograph with no light stain (scale bar 1 µm) of a sinusoid wall viewed from inside the vessel, from a three-week-old wild-type animal. The flat endothelial surface is pitted with many small round fenestrations arranged in sieve-like plates, and arrows mark them. Students should see the dense, regular pores spread across the flat endothelial sheet.

images.title: Neurovascular unit: capillary wall with pericytes, astrocytes and neurons
images.description: Labelled diagram (not a microscope image) of the neurovascular unit in the brain, showing a cross section of a capillary with a single endothelial layer joined by tight junctions, pericytes and basement membrane, surrounded by astrocyte endfeet. Neurons, an interneuron, an astrocyte and microglia sit nearby, and astrocytes signal to the capillary to change blood flow. Students should name the layers of the capillary wall and see how the endothelial tight junctions form the blood-brain barrier.
images.author: Brown LS, Foster CG, Courtney J-M, King NE, Howells DW and Sutherland BA

images.title: Control and diabetic retinal capillaries, showing pericyte loss
images.description: Medical illustration (not a microscope image) comparing a healthy eye with one affected by diabetic retinopathy, with close-ups of retinal capillaries. In the control, the capillary is wrapped by pericytes and carries red blood cells, while in diabetes pericytes are lost or degenerate, leading to microaneurysms, fluid spill and bleeding. Students should identify the pericytes on the capillary and see how losing them weakens the vessel wall.
images.author: Laredo F, Plebanski J and Tedeschi A

tissues.name: Heart valves, endocardium & pericardium
tissues.summary: The heart valves are thin, essentially avascular flaps of dense connective tissue covered by endothelium, opening and closing to keep blood flowing one way through the heart. The endocardium lines the heart chambers and valves, while the epicardium (visceral pericardium) is the outer mesothelial layer over fat and coronary vessels.
features: Valve cusp: fibrosa, spongiosa and ventricularis/atrialis layers of dense connective tissue, essentially avascular
Endocardium: thin endothelial lining over subendothelial connective tissue
Subendocardium: loose connective tissue containing Purkinje fibres, which are large, pale-staining cells
Epicardium (visceral pericardium): mesothelium over fat containing coronary vessels
Rheumatic fever: scarred, fused valve commissures and Aschoff bodies

tissues.name: Lymph node
tissues.summary: The lymph node is an encapsulated organ on the lymphatic route that filters lymph and starts immune responses to the antigens it carries. Its outer cortex holds B-cell follicles, the paracortex holds T cells and high endothelial venules, and the medulla holds cords of plasma cells and medullary sinuses.
features: Thin fibrous capsule with a pale subcapsular sinus just beneath it
Cortex: B-cell follicles, some with pale germinal centres
Paracortex: diffuse T-cell zone with high endothelial venules
Medulla: medullary cords of plasma cells and medullary sinuses
Trabeculae: fibrous septa carrying vessels in from the capsule
Reticular fibres and fibroblastic reticular cells forming a meshwork

tissues.name: Spleen
tissues.summary: The spleen is a lymphoid organ that filters the blood. Its white pulp mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens, while its red pulp removes old and damaged red blood cells.
features: White pulp: lymphoid nodules around central arterioles, with pale germinal centres in B-cell follicles
Marginal zone: a ring of cells at the edge of the white pulp, where it meets the red pulp
Red pulp: splenic cords between wide, blood-filled sinusoids
Sinusoids lined by elongated, stave-like endothelial cells
Fibrous capsule with trabeculae carrying vessels into the organ
Brown haemosiderin pigment in red pulp macrophages

tissues.name: Thymus
tissues.summary: The thymus is the primary lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature, organised into lobules. Each lobule has a dense outer cortex packed with developing thymocytes and a paler medulla containing Hassall's corpuscles.
features: Lobules divided by connective tissue septa, each with a dark cortex and paler medulla
Cortex densely packed with small thymocytes (developing T cells)
Medulla paler, with fewer lymphocytes and more epithelial cells
Hassall's (thymic) corpuscles: concentric whorls of epithelial cells in the medulla
No lymphoid follicles or germinal centres in the normal thymus
Adult thymus involutes, with lymphoid tissue progressively replaced by fat

images.title: Thymus location, lobule histology and cell types (textbook figure)
images.description: Textbook figure from Anatomy & Physiology (Connexions) showing where the thymus lies in the chest, a low-power photomicrograph of a lobule with its capsule, cortex, medulla and trabeculae, and a labelled cartoon of the cell types. The source gives no magnification, and the photomicrograph appears to be H&E stained. Students should match the cortical and medullary cell types in the cartoon to the regions in the photomicrograph.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Cartoon of thymus cell types in cortex and medulla
images.description: Cropped copy of the cartoon panel from the full textbook figure, with the body and photomicrograph panels removed. It shows the fibrous capsule, cortex, medulla, trabeculae, thymocytes, cortical and medullary epithelial cells, dendritic cells, macrophages and a blood vessel. It repeats content already in the full figure, so it adds no new view.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Thymus at low power, H&E section with lobules and septa
images.description: Large low-power H&E section of thymus showing many lobules, each with a darker cortex and a paler medulla, separated by pink connective tissue septa. Dark vertical streaks across the section are most likely folds or mounting artefacts rather than tissue structure. The source gives no magnification, so use it for the lobular pattern and the cortex-medulla contrast.
images.author: Alexander Klepnev

images.title: Wild-type and EphB-deficient thymus: thymocytes and epithelial cells
images.description: Schematic comparing a wild-type (WT) thymus with an EphB-deficient thymus, with blue circles for thymocytes and yellow star shapes for thymic epithelial cells (TECs). The right panel is a research model rather than normal histology, and it shows a different arrangement of the two cell types. It is a diagram, so no stain or magnification applies.
images.author: García-Ceca, J.; Montero-Herradón, S.; Zapata, A.G.

images.title: Thymus location and histology figure, labels in Kurdish
images.description: Kurdish-labelled copy of the textbook thymus figure, showing the same content as the English version: the thymus position in the chest, a low-power lobule section and a cartoon of cell types. The source description is also in Kurdish. It duplicates the English figure, so only the English version needs to be kept.
images.author: Open Stax. https://openstax.org.

images.title: T-cell development stages in the thymic cortex and medulla
images.description: Flow diagram of T lymphocyte development in the thymus, running from early progenitors (ETP/DN1) through DN2, DN3 and DN4 to double-positive cells in the cortex, then to CD4 or CD8 single-positive cells and regulatory T cells (Treg) in the medulla. It is a schematic of stages and signals (such as Notch and pre-TCR), not a stained section, so no stain or magnification applies. Students should learn the order of stages and which steps are beta-selection, positive selection or negative selection.
images.author: Lina Sun, Yanhong Su, Anjun Jiao, Xin Wang

tissues.name: Tonsils (Waldeyer's ring)
tissues.summary: The tonsils are partially encapsulated lymphoid tissues lying beneath the pharyngeal epithelium as part of Waldeyer's ring. The palatine tonsil is lined by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium that dips into crypts, while the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid) is covered by respiratory epithelium.
features: Palatine tonsil: non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium dipping into deep crypts
Numerous lymphoid follicles with pale germinal centres and dark mantle zones
Tingible body macrophages with apoptotic debris inside germinal centres
Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid): covered by pseudostratified ciliated respiratory epithelium

images.title: Tonsil locations in the head, and histology of the palatine tonsil
images.description: A textbook figure with panel a showing line drawings of the head with the palatine, pharyngeal and lingual tonsils, plus a photograph of the open mouth with swollen palatine tonsils. Panel b is a low-power H&E micrograph of a palatine tonsil, with a crypt, stratified squamous epithelium and germinal centres labelled. Students should match the tonsil positions in panel a with the histology in panel b.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Stratified squamous epithelium above gland acini in an eyepiece view
images.description: Circular microscope-field photograph stained with H&E, showing stratified squamous epithelium with a fold on the right and rounded gland acini in the connective tissue on the left. No lymphoid follicles are clear in this field, so it is a weak guide to tonsil and students should rely on the other images for follicles. The source gives no magnification.
images.author: Нужина Дарья

tissues.name: Thin (hairy) skin
tissues.summary: Thin (hairy) skin covers most of the body: a keratinised stratified squamous epidermis with no stratum lucidum sits over a dermis of papillary and reticular connective tissue that contains hair follicles and glands, with a hypodermis of adipose tissue beneath. It protects the body and, through its sensory receptors, hair, sweat glands and blood supply, helps detect touch and temperature and regulate body heat.
features: Keratinised stratified squamous epidermis with no stratum lucidum
Hair follicles with hair shafts, sebaceous glands and arrector pili muscles in the dermis
Papillary dermis of loose connective tissue above reticular dermis of dense irregular connective tissue
Melanocytes in the basal layer, which pass melanin to the keratinocytes
Sweat glands and blood vessels in the dermis
Hypodermis of adipose tissue beneath the dermis

images.title: Skin layers in H&E: epidermis, papillary dermis and reticular dermis
images.description: Labelled H&E section of thin skin, with arrows marking the epidermis, the papillary dermis and the reticular dermis. The keratinised epidermis sits on loose papillary dermis, which grades into the denser reticular dermis below. Students should trace where the papillary layer ends and the reticular layer begins.
images.author:

images.title: Hair follicles in skin with a skeletal muscle layer beneath, in H&E
images.description: Large section of hairy skin, which appears to be H&E stained, with several hair follicles running down into the dermis and each showing its hair shaft and bulb. A band of skeletal muscle lies across the base of the field, beneath the dermis. The source gives neither species nor magnification, so the follicles and the muscle layer are the landmarks to use.
images.author: Pathologist without beard

images.title: Papillary and reticular layers of the dermis, labelled micrograph
images.description: Labelled micrograph of skin, which the source describes as an illustration, although it is a stained section and the colours suggest H&E. The bracket marks the papillary layer just beneath the epidermis, and the label marks the reticular layer of denser collagen below it. Students should compare the looser papillary layer with the reticular layer.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Dermal circulation: 3D diagram of skin layers and blood supply
images.description: 3D medical illustration of a block of skin showing the papillary and reticular layers of the dermis, with the papillary plexus, dermal papillae, capillary loops, a hair and its follicle, and the cutaneous plexus at the base. It is a diagram rather than a stained section. Use it to link the layers of the dermis to their blood supply.
images.author:
BruceBlaus. When using this image in external sources it can be cited as:

images.title: Historical image of a single dendritic (Langerhans) cell with branching processes
images.description: Black and white image of a single cell with long branching processes, captioned as a dendritic cell by Paul Langerhans. The source gives no stain or magnification. It shows a Langerhans cell, an epidermal dendritic cell, rather than an islet cell, so it belongs with the skin.
images.author: w:Paul Langerhans

images.title: Schematic of a Langerhans cell in the epidermis, macrophage and dendritic features
images.description: Diagram, not a micrograph, of the epidermis from the stratum basale to the stratum corneum, with a Langerhans cell in the stratum spinosum. Green labels mark macrophage features such as self-renewal and embryonic origin, and red labels mark dendritic cell features such as antigen presentation and migration to lymph nodes. No stain, as it is a diagram.
images.author: Deckers J, Hammad H and Hoste E

images.title: Langerhans cell roles in the skin and after migration to the lymph node
images.description: Figure 1 diagram, not a micrograph, comparing Langerhans cell functions in the skin (left, within the epidermis) with migratory functions in a lymph node (right). Green boxes mark known functions and red boxes mark potential functions, and the T cell types involved are shown in the key. It is a diagram of skin immunology, not of islets, so it belongs with the skin.
images.author: West HC and Bennett CL

images.title: Langerhans cells in epidermal sheets and their dendrite counts
images.description: Figure 3 with a micrograph of two Langerhans cells in epidermal sheets (panel A, scale bar 10 micrometres), where brown cell processes stand out against a blue-purple background, and bar charts of dendrites per cell (panels B to D). The stain is not named in the source. Students should count the dendrites on cells i and ii, and see how counts differ between untreated and treated skin and between pre-culture and post-culture at 24 and 48 hours.
images.author: M, Kang S-M, Song J-M, Anstey AV, Ivory M, Compans RW, et al.

tissues.name: Thick (glabrous) skin
tissues.summary: Thick, hairless skin of the palms and soles, with a very thick keratinised epidermis that has five layers, including a stratum lucidum. Its thick epidermis and deep epidermal ridges resist friction and abrasion on these weight-bearing surfaces.
features: Very thick stratum corneum with a distinct, pale stratum lucidum beneath it
Deep epidermal ridges (rete pegs) projecting between dermal papillae
No hair follicles or sebaceous glands in the section
Eccrine sweat ducts coiling through the epidermis
Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae, close under the basal layer
structures: Palmar surfaces of digits of hand
Plantar surfaces of digits of foot

images.title: Thick skin (a) compared with thin skin (b), H&E sections
images.description: Two micrographs labelled (a) and (b), each with a small low-power inset, appearing to be H&E-stained; no magnification is given. Panel (a) is thick skin, with a broad, dark epidermis under a keratinised surface layer and deep, thick epidermal ridges reaching into the dermis. Panel (b) is thin skin, with a flat epidermis only a few cells thick over dense pink dermis, so students can compare the depth of the ridges and the thickness of the epidermis.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Thick skin epidermis: labelled diagram of its five layers
images.description: Labelled teaching diagram of a section through thick skin, from the dermis up to the stratum corneum. It shows the five epidermal layers in order (stratum basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum and corneum), with keratin-filled dead cells at the surface, and the melanocyte, Merkel cell and sensory neuron in the basal region. Students should learn the order of the layers and that the stratum lucidum is found in thick skin.
images.author: OpenStax College : J. Gordon Betts, Peter Desaix, Eddie Johnson.

images.title: Finger pad skin (thick, hairless skin) at large magnification
images.description: Skin of the finger pad at large magnification, with no stain given in the source; the colours suggest H&E. Most of the field is pale polygonal cells with thin pink walls that look like fat cells, with a blood vessel at lower right and dark-staining strands; no epidermis is in view. Finger pad skin is thick skin, so this image belongs with the thick skin tissue rather than thin skin.
images.author: Глущенко Арина

images.title: Finger pad skin (thick, hairless skin) at small magnification
images.description: Skin of the finger pad at small magnification, with no stain given in the source; the colours suggest H&E. A thick layer of keratin and the epidermis lie along the lower edge, with dark-staining cell clusters and white fat cells in the dermis above, so the full thickness of the skin is visible. No hair follicles are in view, so this is thick skin and belongs with the thick skin tissue.
images.author: Глущенко Арина

images.title: Finger pad skin (thick, hairless skin) at medium magnification
images.description: Skin of the finger pad at medium magnification, with no stain given in the source; the colours suggest H&E. The field shows white fat cells at top left, dark-staining cell clusters, a blood vessel with a wavy wall at right and dense pink connective tissue, with no epidermis in view. It is thick skin rather than thin skin, so it belongs with the thick skin tissue.
images.author: Глущенко Арина

tissues.name: Hair follicle & sebaceous gland
tissues.summary: The hair follicle is a down-growth of epidermis into the dermis that makes the hair shaft from matrix cells at its bulb, which caps the dermal papilla. Attached sebaceous glands release sebum into the follicle, and arrector pili smooth muscle erects the hair.
features: Hair bulb: matrix cells capping the dermal papilla at the base of the follicle
Hair shaft: keratinised central core, often pale in sections
Inner and outer root sheaths: nucleated epithelium wrapping the hair shaft
Sebaceous glands: clusters of pale, foamy cells opening into the follicle
Arrector pili: thin smooth muscle band running from the follicle to the dermis
Bulge: swelling of the outer root sheath where follicular stem cells sit

images.title: Hair follicle and sebaceous gland diagram with micrograph (English labels)
images.description: Teaching figure with a skin schematic and an H&E-stained micrograph of a hair follicle with its sebaceous gland, labelled in English for the hair, epidermis and sebaceous gland. The source calls it an illustration from an Anatomy and Physiology textbook (Connexions), and it is the same figure as the Spanish-labelled version. Students should match the schematic to the micrograph and find the hair shaft, sebaceous lobules and follicle wall.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Hair follicle cut lengthwise, showing the hair shaft and adjacent fat
images.description: H&E-stained photomicrograph of a hair follicle in longitudinal section, with the dark hair shaft running diagonally through it and pale fat cells beside it. The source calls it an illustration, but it looks like a photographic micrograph, and no magnification is given. Students should find the hair shaft, the surrounding root sheath and the fat cells.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Hair follicle and surrounding epidermis, immunofluorescence stains
images.description: Three-part fluorescence micrograph of skin with antibody stains and a DAPI nuclear stain (blue); the left panel shows CD34 (green) and keratin 14 (red), and the right panel shows AE13 (green), Ki67 (red) and beta4 (white). The source gives no magnification. Students should find the bulge, sebaceous gland, dermal papilla, matrix cells, and the inner and outer root sheaths.
images.author: Gaelle, L. and Cédric, B., Medical applications of epidermal stem cells (November 15, 2008), StemBook, ed. The Stem Cell Research Community, StemBook, doi/10.3824/stembook.1.27.1, http://www.stembook.

tissues.name: Sweat glands
tissues.summary: Sweat glands are exocrine glands in the dermis that release sweat through ducts onto the skin surface. Eccrine glands, found over most of the body, produce watery sweat for thermoregulation, while apocrine glands in the axilla and groin open into hair follicles.
features: Eccrine secretory coil: a coiled tube of clear and dark cells, with myoepithelial cells around it, lying deep in the dermis
Eccrine duct: two layers of cuboidal cells that stain darker than the secretory coil, running up to the epidermis
Apocrine gland: wide lumens with secretion pinched off from the apical part of the cell
Apocrine glands open into the upper part of hair follicles rather than onto the skin surface
Myoepithelial cells: flattened contractile cells lying outside the secretory cells of both gland types

images.title: Skin cutaway showing an eccrine sweat gland and its pore
images.description: Cutaway illustration of skin showing a hair follicle, an eccrine sweat gland coil in the lower dermis near the fat, and its duct rising to a pore on the skin surface. It is a diagram, so no stain or magnification applies. Students should trace the duct from the coil up to the pore and compare it with the hair follicle beside it.
images.author: OpenStax College

images.title: Axillary skin with apocrine and eccrine sweat glands
images.description: Three-panel figure of axillary (armpit) skin, and the stain appears to be H&E. Panel a is a low-power view (scale bar 3000 µm) with the dermis, a sweat gland layer and fat marked. Panels b and c (scale bars 30 µm) show an apocrine gland with secretory blebs (arrowheads) and secretory products (arrow) in the secretory coil, and the secretory coil of an eccrine gland, which has two cell layers and is covered with myoepithelial cells.
images.author: Shinaoka A, Nakahara R, Saeki M

images.title: Skin section showing sweat gland ducts and coiled glands
images.description: Engraved line drawing of a vertical section of skin, with the sweat gland ducts shown in orange: the ducts run up through the epidermis to the surface, and the coiled secretory glands lie in the deeper dermis and fat. It is a diagram, so no stain or magnification applies. Students should trace a duct from its coil up through the epidermal layers to the stratum corneum, and note the adipose tissue, artery and nerve around the glands.
images.author: Henry Gray

labels.text: Coiled secretory portion of sweat gland

tissues.name: Skin sensory receptors
tissues.summary: Sensory receptors of the skin that respond to touch, pressure, vibration and stretch. Most are encapsulated mechanoreceptor endings in the dermis and hypodermis, such as the Meissner, Pacinian and Ruffini corpuscles.
features: Meissner corpuscle: small oval of stacked flattened cells filling a dermal papilla just beneath the epidermis
Pacinian corpuscle: large onion-like rings of concentric lamellae around a central core, in the deep dermis or hypodermis
Ruffini ending: spindle-shaped capsule in the dermis with branching nerve endings inside
Dermal papillae: finger-like dermal projections pushing up into the epidermis, where the Meissner corpuscles sit
Adipose tissue: Pacinian corpuscles lie among fat cells and small blood vessels in the hypodermis

images.title: Pacinian corpuscle in cross-section, showing concentric lamellae
images.description: Section stained with H&E, judging by the pink and purple colouring. The source gives no magnification or site. A large Pacinian corpuscle appears as a ring of concentric lamellae around a small central core, with fat and fibrous tissue beside it. Students should look for the layered capsule and the central core.

images.title: Meissner corpuscle at the tip of a dermal papilla, H&E section
images.description: Thick skin section stained with H&E at 100x magnification, as given by the source. The arrow points to a Meissner corpuscle at the tip of a dermal papilla, under a thick stratum corneum. Students should find the oval corpuscle of stacked cells within the papilla, just beneath the epidermis.
images.author: Wbensmith

images.title: Several Pacinian corpuscles among adipose tissue, H&E section
images.description: H&E stained section at 40x magnification, as given by the source, showing several Pacinian corpuscles cut in cross-section. The corpuscles sit among clusters of fat cells, with small blood vessels and fibrous tissue around them. Students should find the concentric lamellae of each corpuscle, which are much larger than the vessels nearby.
images.author: Wbensmith

images.title: Pacinian corpuscle in skin: 3D cutaway diagram with close-up inset
images.description: Coloured 3D medical illustration of a skin block with hair shafts and several nerve endings, labelled in Spanish as Corpúsculo de Pacini. A boxed inset enlarges one corpuscle, an onion-like stack of lamellae around a central core with a nerve fibre, lying in the fatty hypodermis. Students should see that the corpuscle sits deep in the skin, well below the epidermis.
images.author: BruceBlaus

images.title: Ruffini corpuscle in skin: 3D cutaway diagram with close-up inset
images.description: Coloured 3D medical illustration of a skin block with hair shafts and several nerve endings, labelled Ruffini Corpuscle. A boxed inset enlarges a lens-shaped capsule lying in the dermis, with branching nerve endings inside it and a nerve fibre entering from below. Students should note that the capsule is elongated and lies roughly parallel to the skin surface.

tissues.name: Nail
tissues.summary: The nail is a plate of hard keratin on the dorsal tip of each finger and toe, protecting the distal digit and supporting fine touch and grip. It is produced by the nail matrix under the proximal nail fold, and the plate slides forward over the nail bed.
features: Nail plate: compact layers of hard keratin with no visible nuclei
Nail matrix: proliferating epidermis under the proximal nail fold that produces the plate
Nail bed: thin epidermis lacking a granular layer, sitting on a dermis with longitudinal ridges
Eponychium: thin keratinised layer of the proximal nail fold that seals the nail root
Lunula: pale crescent at the base of the plate, the visible distal matrix

images.title: Nail and nail groove: longitudinal section diagram
images.description: Labelled line drawing of a longitudinal section through the nail and its nail groove (sulcus), with the eponychium at the proximal fold. It is a drawing rather than a microscope image, so there is no stain or magnification. Students should trace the nail plate within its groove, the epidermal layers (stratum corneum, stratum granulosum, stratum mucosum), and the blood vessels in the corium.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Lip & oral mucosa
tissues.summary: Lip and oral mucosa is the moist, stratified squamous lining of the mouth, resting on a lamina propria of connective tissue. It protects the underlying tissue from friction and microbes, changing from keratinised skin on the outer lip to non-keratinised lining inside the mouth.
features: Skin side of the lip: hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands
Vermilion border: thin keratinised epithelium with tall papillae bringing capillaries close to the surface (red colour)
Inner lip (mucosa): non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium with minor salivary glands
Gingiva and hard palate: keratinised masticatory mucosa bound firmly to bone

tissues.name: Tongue & taste buds
tissues.summary: The tongue is a muscular organ whose upper surface is covered by stratified squamous epithelium forming papillae, and many of these papillae carry taste buds. Its interlacing skeletal muscle moves food during chewing and swallowing and helps shape speech.
features: Filiform papillae: conical and keratinised, with no taste buds, and the most numerous papillae
Fungiform papillae: mushroom-shaped, with taste buds on the top surface
Circumvallate papillae: large, set in a trench, with taste buds in its walls and serous von Ebner glands at its base
Foliate papillae: folds on the posterolateral margins, with taste buds in their walls
Interlacing skeletal muscle fibres in three planes, cut lengthways and in cross section
Taste buds: pale barrel-shaped clusters of gustatory and supporting cells, opening through a taste pore

images.title: Tongue dorsal surface with labelled tissue layers, H&E
images.description: Annotated H&E-stained section of the dorsal (upper) surface of the tongue, with coloured lines marking epithelium, connective tissue, muscle and a glandular zone. Students should find the epithelial papillae along the top, the connective tissue cores inside them and the interlacing skeletal muscle below. The green glandular label does not clearly match any glands in this field.
images.author: Otávio Astor Vaz Costa

images.title: Tongue muscle bundles beside papillary epithelium, H&E
images.description: H&E-stained section of the tongue, as the source states, with no scale bar. Skeletal muscle fibres, cut in longitudinal and cross section, run in bundles separated by thin connective tissue septa, and stratified squamous epithelium with papillae lies at the upper right. Students should compare the pink muscle fibres with the purple epithelium and the connective tissue core of its papillae.
images.author: Alexander Klepnev

images.title: Tongue epithelium with papillae and striated muscle, H&E
images.description: H&E-stained section of the tongue, as the source states, with no scale bar. Stratified squamous epithelium forms papillae on the right, with connective tissue below, while skeletal muscle fibres fill the lower left in longitudinal and cross section. Students should identify the papillae of the epithelium and separate them from the muscle bundles beside them.
images.author: Alexander Klepnev

images.title: Striated muscle of the tongue with lingual glands, H&E
images.description: H&E-type section of tongue striated muscle, cut in longitudinal and cross section, with purple lingual gland acini lying between the bundles. A duct-like structure runs through the lower middle of the field. Students should separate the long pink fibres from the polygonal cross sections and find the gland acini between the muscle bundles.
images.author: Molecularu

images.title: Tongue muscle bundles with lingual gland acini, H&E
images.description: H&E-type section of tongue striated muscle with purple gland acini (lingual salivary glands) lying between the pink muscle bundles. A duct-like profile with a central lumen sits at the lower right of the field. Students should separate the purple acini from the pink fibres and find this duct.
images.author: Molecularu

images.title: Tongue papillae types and taste bud structure, labelled diagram
images.description: Labelled diagram of the upper tongue surface showing fungiform, filiform, foliate and circumvallate papillae, with an inset micrograph of a taste bud in a circumvallate papilla. A separate enlargement of a taste bud labels the taste hairs, taste pore, and basal, gustatory and transitional cells. Students should learn which papillae carry taste buds and where each type sits on the tongue.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Coronal section of the tongue showing its intrinsic muscles
images.description: Black and white Gray's Anatomy drawing, altered from Krause, of a coronal section through the tongue. It is a gross anatomy drawing rather than a microscope view, and labels the superior and inferior longitudinal muscles, the transverse muscle, the vertical fibres of the genioglossus, the septum, the papillae and the lingual artery. Students should see how the muscle fibres interlace in three planes within the body of the tongue.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Tooth
tissues.summary: The tooth is a mineralised organ for cutting and grinding food, built from enamel, dentine and cementum around a vascular pulp. It sits in a bony socket and is anchored there by the periodontal ligament, forming a gomphosis joint.
features: Enamel: highly mineralised and acellular, lost in decalcified sections
Dentine: pale, with fine tubules containing odontoblast processes
Pulp: loose connective tissue with blood vessels and nerves at the centre
Cementum: thin layer on the root surface, pale and acellular in sections
Developing tooth: enamel organ around a dental papilla at the bud, cap and bell stages

images.title: Stages of tooth development from placode to root formation
images.description: A composite figure of five stained micrographs (appears H&E) showing placode, bud, cap, late bell and root stages. Printed labels mark the epithelium and mesenchyme, stellate reticulum, enamel knot, dental papilla, dental follicle, ameloblasts, enamel, dentine, odontoblasts, crown, root, cell rests of Malassez and Hertwig's epithelial root sheath. The figure shows that the crown forms before root formation starts.
images.author: Thesleff, I. and Tummers, M., Tooth organogenesis and regeneration (January 31, 2009), StemBook, ed. The Stem Cell Research Community, StemBook, doi/10.3824/stembook.1.37.1, http://www.stembook.org.

images.title: Tooth enamel surface in a scanning electron microscope
images.description: A scanning electron micrograph, with no stain, which the source describes as tooth enamel. At the magnification shown on the image (148x, 1 mm scale bar) the fractured surface looks cracked and terraced, and no individual enamel prisms are resolved. It shows surface fracture and layering rather than a stained section.
images.author: Вовк Сузанна

tissues.name: Parotid gland
tissues.summary: The parotid gland is a purely serous salivary gland that secretes watery, amylase-rich saliva through a branching duct system into the mouth.
features: Serous acini with basal basophilia and apical zymogen granules
Prominent intercalated and striated ducts between the acini
Connective tissue septa dividing the gland into lobules
Adipocytes that increase in number with age
Facial nerve branches running through the gland

images.title: Parotid gland: duct and serous acini in H&E section
images.description: Parotid gland in a section that appears to be H&E stained; the source gives no magnification. Duct profiles with pale lumens and a cuboidal to columnar lining sit in loose connective tissue on the left, while the closely packed serous acini on the right have granular, pink-purple cytoplasm and round nuclei. Students should compare the paler ducts with the denser acini and note the fibrous connective tissue separating them.
images.author: Wbensmith

images.title: Salivary gland: glandular profiles with pale lumens, eyepiece photo
images.description: Circular microscope field photographed through the eyepiece, with a pink-purple stain that looks like H&E; the source gives only 'salivary gland' and no magnification. Several pale lumens are surrounded by cells with round nuclei, but the field is soft and vignetted at the edges, so acinar and ductal profiles cannot be told apart with confidence. Students should look for the glandular lumens and nuclei here rather than fine cellular detail.
images.author: Нужина Дарья

tissues.name: Submandibular gland
tissues.summary: The submandibular gland is a paired major salivary gland beneath the floor of the mouth, and its mixed secretion, mostly serous, drains into the mouth through the submandibular (Wharton's) duct. Its secretory units are mainly serous acini with some mucous tubules capped by serous demilunes, and long striated ducts modify the saliva as it passes along them.
features: Serous acini: rounded clusters of cells with basophilic (purple-staining) cytoplasm
Mucous acini and tubules: pale, clear-staining cytoplasm
Serous demilunes: crescent-shaped caps of serous cells over mucous units (the caps can be partly a fixation artefact)
Long striated ducts with fine basal striations running through the lobules
Fat-rich connective tissue between lobules, with ducts and blood vessels

images.title: Submandibular gland: mixed mucous and serous acini with a duct
images.description: H&E-type stained section of submandibular gland, as far as can be judged, showing lobules of mixed secretory acini. Pale mucous acini sit beside darker serous acini, and fibrous connective tissue separates the lobules. A duct with a central lumen lies in the connective tissue at the lower centre, and fat cells are at the upper right; the source gives no magnification.
images.author: Wbensmith

images.title: Myoepithelial cells around acini, alpha-smooth muscle actin stain
images.description: Immunohistochemistry for alpha-smooth muscle actin, shown as brown staining with a blue nuclear counterstain, highlighting myoepithelial cells (arrows) that wrap round secretory acini. The source describes a strong positive reaction and gives a 20 micrometre scale bar, but it does not name the organ. Students should look for the flattened brown cells on the outside of the acini, which contract to push secretion out.
images.author: El Sadik A., Mohamed E., El Zainy A.

images.title: Submandibular gland: serous and mucous acini, textbook diagram
images.description: Engraved textbook drawing of a human submaxillary (submandibular) gland, credited to R. Heidenhain, showing lobules in section. The caption places the mucous alveoli on the right and the serous alveoli on the left, and the drawing matches this: the stippled, dark units on the left are serous, while the pale, clear units on the right are mucous. It is a line drawing, so no stain or magnification applies, and the fibrous septa outlining each lobule are clearly drawn.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Sublingual gland
tissues.summary: The sublingual gland is a mixed salivary gland beneath the tongue in the floor of the mouth, producing mainly viscous mucous saliva that lubricates the oral cavity. Its acini are dominated by pale mucous cells, with only a few serous demilunes, and its ducts are short and hard to see.
features: Mostly mucous acini with pale, foamy cytoplasm and flattened basal nuclei
Few serous demilunes capping some mucous acini
Short, inconspicuous striated ducts
Lobules separated by thin connective tissue septa carrying ducts and vessels

tissues.name: Oesophagus
tissues.summary: The oesophagus is a muscular tube that carries food from the pharynx to the stomach. Its wall has a thick, non-keratinised stratified squamous lining, submucosal mucous glands, and a muscle coat that changes from skeletal muscle at the top to smooth muscle at the bottom.
features: Thick non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, with nuclei still visible in the surface cells
Lamina propria papillae pushing up into the epithelium
Submucosal mucous glands with pale acini and ducts
Muscularis externa: skeletal muscle in the upper third, smooth muscle in the lower third
Adventitia (loose connective tissue) rather than serosa in the chest part
Lymphoid aggregates in the lamina propria and submucosa

images.title: Oesophageal lining fold with submucosal glands (eyepiece photo)
images.description: A photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece of a section of the oesophageal wall in a pink and purple stain, probably H&E; the source gives no magnification. A fold of lining epithelium borders a pale space, and the loose connective tissue on the right holds rounded gland acini. The image is soft and has a colour cast, so the cell detail is limited.
images.author: Abdulrazakca

images.title: Schematic cross-section of the oesophageal wall (diagram)
images.description: A schematic cross-section of the oesophageal wall drawn as a circle, with a folded lining along the top. It shows the stratified squamous lining, submucosal glands and blood vessels, a band of muscle, and an outer layer of connective tissue. Arrows point to these parts, but the text labels are cut off at the edge, so students must name them.
images.author: DrJanaOfficial

images.title: Trachea and oesophagus in lung tissue at low power (H&E)
images.description: H&E section at low power, as the source states, showing the trachea and oesophagus with the surrounding lung. The lung appears as pale air spaces with thin walls, and a round vessel full of red blood cells sits near the tubes. The wall detail is too coarse to pick out clearly, so students should use this image for the position of the tubes rather than their layers.
images.author: Otávio Astor Vaz Costa

images.title: Oesophageal wall in trichrome stain: epithelium, collagen and muscle
images.description: A transverse section in a trichrome-type stain, which appears to colour collagen blue and muscle and epithelium red; the source gives no magnification. The orange-red stratified epithelium forms a wavy lining along the top, with blue collagen-rich connective tissue beneath it and red muscle bundles with pale rounded areas at the lower right. Students should compare the blue connective tissue layer with the red muscle.
images.author: Lorenzo Apolloni

images.title: Oesophagus wall in transverse section: labelled drawing
images.description: An engraved line drawing of a transverse section of the human oesophagus, made from a drawing by V. Horsley and shown at moderate magnification, as stated in the source. Letters mark the fibrous covering (a), the longitudinal and transverse muscle coats (b and c), the submucous or areolar layer (d), the muscularis mucosae (e), the mucosa with a lymphoid nodule (f) and the stratified epithelium (g). It is an accurate diagram of the oesophagus wall, where the areolar layer is only one labelled part, so it does not depict loose connective tissue on its own.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Gastro-oesophageal junction
tissues.summary: The gastro-oesophageal junction is the transition zone where the non-keratinised squamous lining of the oesophagus meets the columnar mucosa of the stomach, marked by the Z-line. The cardiac mucosa just inside the stomach holds coiled glands that secrete mucus.
features: Sharp Z-line where the squamous lining of the oesophagus meets columnar gastric mucosa
Cardiac glands: coiled, mucus-secreting tubular glands in the proximal stomach mucosa
Goblet cells above the junction: intestinal metaplasia, as in Barrett oesophagus
Muscularis mucosae forming the smooth muscle layer beneath the glands

images.title: Cardiac region of the stomach: cardiac glands and their ducts in section
images.description: Historical engraving from Gray's Anatomy showing a section of human stomach mucous membrane near the cardiac orifice, drawn by v. Ebner after J. Schaffer at x45 magnification. The stain is not stated, as it is a drawn engraving rather than a photomicrograph. Students should find the folded mucosa, the coiled cardiac glands and their ducts, a gland with goblet cells similar to intestinal glands, and the muscularis mucosae at the base.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Stomach (fundus & body)
tissues.summary: The stomach's inner lining (gastric mucosa) of the fundus and body is built from shallow gastric pits and long oxyntic glands. Its parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, and its chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which starts protein digestion.
features: Surface mucous cells: simple columnar epithelium lining the shallow gastric pits, with no goblet cells
Oxyntic glands: long tubular glands below the pits in the fundus and body
Parietal cells: large, round, pink (eosinophilic) cells with a central round nucleus, mainly in the middle and upper glands
Chief cells: purple (basophilic) cells with dark nuclei, clustered at the bases of the glands
Muscularis externa: three muscle layers, with an inner oblique layer, seen in the wall at low power

images.title: Chief cell of the gastric gland, electron micrograph
images.description: Electron micrograph of a chief cell from the body (corpus) of the gastric mucosa, so no stain applies, with a 2 µm scale bar. The well-developed Golgi apparatus lies above the nucleus, and many secretory granules of varying size and density fill the supranuclear cytoplasm, with the gland lumen at the upper left. A student should find the bipolar cell organisation, its Golgi and the dense granules packed above the nucleus.
images.author: Natalia Ziółkowska , Bogdan Lewczuk , Wojciech Petryński , Katarzyna Palkowska , Magdalena Prusik , Krystyna Targońska , Zygmunt Giżejewski , Barbara Przybylska-Gornowicz.

images.title: Neck of a gastric gland with mucous, parietal and chief cells
images.description: Electron micrograph of the neck of a gastric gland in the body of the stomach, with a 5 µm scale bar and no stain. Mucous neck cells (M) lie at the top left, a parietal cell (P) is on the right, and a chief cell (C) lies lower down, with the gland lumen (L) near the centre. Arrows mark bipartite secretory granules in the mucous neck cells, and the asterisk marks stacks of rough endoplasmic reticulum in the chief cell.
images.author: Natalia Ziółkowska , Bogdan Lewczuk , Wojciech Petryński , Katarzyna Palkowska , Magdalena Prusik , Krystyna Targońska , Zygmunt Giżejewski , Barbara Przybylska-Gornowicz.

images.title: Human gastric glands with parietal and chief cells, light micrograph
images.description: Light micrograph of human gastric glands, photographed through a microscope with a digital camera, with no magnification given. The stain appears to be H&E: large pink parietal cells with round central nuclei sit among purple chief cells in the glands, and loose connective tissue with small nuclei lies between them. A student should find the pink parietal cells and the purple chief cells, and tell them apart by cytoplasm colour and nucleus appearance.
images.author: Jpogi at English Wikipedia

images.title: Parietal cell beside chief cells, close-up light micrograph
images.description: Close-up light micrograph with an H&E-type pink and purple stain, with no magnification given, and labels reading 'Parietal cell' and 'Chief cells' in the image. The labels mark the large pink cell with a round central nucleus as the parietal cell, and the purple cells with dark nuclei as chief cells. A student should compare the rounded, pink parietal cytoplasm with the darker purple chief cells.
images.author:
Mikael Häggström, M.D. Author info

images.title: Stomach fundus wall, low-power H&E section
images.description: Low-power H&E light micrograph of a section through the wall of the stomach, captioned in the source as the bottom (fundus) of the stomach; no magnification is given. The purple mucosa forms one band, a thin pinkish submucosa lies beside it, and the thick muscular coat forms the broad band on the opposite side. A student should identify these three layers of the wall in one view.
images.author: Alexander Klepnev

images.title: Pyloric region of the stomach wall, light micrograph
images.description: Light micrograph photographed through a microscope eyepiece, captioned in the source as the pyloric part of the stomach, with no magnification given and the stain not stated (the pink-red colour suggests an eosin-based stain). The mucosa with its gastric pits forms the top of the field, a band of connective tissue with small vessels (submucosa) lies below, and the thick muscular coat fills the bottom. A student should identify these three layers and the pits in the mucosa, although the blur and circular field make fine detail hard to see.
images.author: Нужина Дарья

images.title: Parietal cell in a gastric gland neck, electron micrograph
images.description: Electron micrograph of a parietal cell (marked P) in a longitudinal section through the neck of a gastric gland, with no stain and no scale bar shown. The round nucleus sits at the top, and the cytoplasm is packed with mitochondria around branching intracellular canaliculi, which appear as channel-like profiles. A student should find the canaliculi and the mitochondria-rich cytoplasm that mark an acid-secreting parietal cell.
images.author: Natalia Ziółkowska , Bogdan Lewczuk , Wojciech Petryński , Katarzyna Palkowska , Magdalena Prusik , Krystyna Targońska , Zygmunt Giżejewski , Barbara Przybylska-Gornowicz

images.title: Parietal cell with well-developed tubulovesicular system, electron micrograph
images.description: Electron micrograph of a parietal cell (labelled D) at low magnification, with a 2 µm scale bar and no stain. The source describes a well-developed tubulovesicular system, which appears here as a pale, membrane-rich cluster of tubules and vesicles in the cytoplasm, with the round nucleus below it. A student should find this pale network set among the dense mitochondria.
images.author: Natalia Ziółkowska , Bogdan Lewczuk , Wojciech Petryński , Katarzyna Palkowska , Magdalena Prusik , Krystyna Targońska , Zygmunt Giżejewski , Barbara Przybylska-Gornowicz

images.title: Gastric glands of the stomach body in a beaver, light micrograph
images.description: Light micrograph of the body region of a beaver stomach, as captioned in the source, with the stain appearing to be H&E and no magnification given. Pink parietal cells with round central nuclei lie among purple-staining chief cells, and small dark nuclei of connective tissue lie between the glands. Because this is beaver tissue, a student should compare the cell arrangement with human material rather than treat it as human.
images.author: Natalia Ziółkowska, Bogdan Lewczuk, Wojciech Petryński, Katarzyna Palkowska, Magdalena Prusik, Krystyna Targońska, Zygmunt Giżejewski, Barbara Przybylska-Gornowicz

images.title: Resting parietal cell from a rat, electron micrograph
images.description: Small electron micrograph of a resting parietal cell from a rat, treated with cimetidine and prepared by high-pressure freezing, with a 2 µm scale bar given in the source. The source describes narrow intracellular canaliculi and numerous tubules and vesicles in the cytoplasm, but at this small size these are hard to resolve, and the central nucleus is the main clear feature. The low resolution makes it of limited use for showing fine structure.
images.author: Fumiyo Aoyama , Akira Sawaguchi

tissues.name: Pyloric antrum
tissues.summary: The pyloric antrum is the distal part of the stomach, lined by mucus-secreting mucosa with deep gastric pits and short, coiled mucous glands. Its G cells secrete gastrin, which drives acid secretion, and a thickened circular muscle forms the pyloric sphincter that guards the duodenum.
features: Deep gastric pits, roughly half the mucosal depth
Short, coiled, branched mucous glands with pale mucus-filled cells
G cells (gastrin-secreting) at the gland bases, best shown by gastrin immunostaining
No parietal or chief cells in the glands, unlike the fundus
Thick circular muscle layer forming the pyloric sphincter

images.title: Antral gastric mucosa: surface pits and deep coiled mucous glands
images.description: Section through antral gastric mucosa, H&E stained at 10x, with a 40x inset in the lower right. The surface is lined by tall columnar cells forming deep pits, and the coiled glands below are filled with pale mucus-secreting cells. In the inset, look for pale cytoplasm with flattened basal nuclei, which is typical of mucous cells.
images.author: Carrasco G, Corvalan AH

images.title: Fundic gastric mucosa: surface pits and deep acid-secreting glands
images.description: H&E section of fundic gastric mucosa at 10x, with a 40x inset in the lower right. The surface is folded into pits, and the deeper glands are lined by cells with pale cytoplasm. In the inset, the large rounded cells with central nuclei and pink cytoplasm appear to be parietal cells.
images.author: Carrasco G, Corvalan AH

images.title: Foveolar cells: mucus-secreting lining of a gastric pit
images.description: High-power H&E view of foveolar (surface mucous) cells lining a gastric pit, from the antrum according to the source. The tall columnar cells have pale, mucus-rich cytoplasm and dark oval nuclei set towards the base, and the open pit lumen shows as a white channel. Red blood cells sit in the lamina propria at the left.

images.title: ECL cells in Grimelius silver stain of gastric mucosa
images.description: Gastric mucosa stained by the Grimelius silver method, with ECL cells appearing dark brown to black against a yellow-orange background. Panel C is at medium power with a 50 micrometre scale bar, and the boxed area is enlarged in panel D with a 10 micrometre scale bar. The source labels panel C as antral mucosa, and students should look for the dark cells lying along the gland walls.
images.author: Maksud F.A.N. , Kakehasi A.M. , Barbosa A.J.A.

images.title: Gastric glands in antrum and corpus, with cell-type diagram
images.description: Composite figure with H&E sections of the antrum (top left) and corpus (top right), schematic gastric glands below each, and a stomach outline marking the pylorus, antrum, corpus, fundus and cardia. The schematics are colour-coded by cell type, including surface mucous, mucous neck, parietal, chief, G, ECL and stem cells, with molecular markers in blue text. In the antral gland, G cells sit at the base, and the schematic shows no parietal or chief cells.
images.author: Shiyu Xiao , Liya Zhou

tissues.name: Duodenum
tissues.summary: The duodenum is the first part of the small intestine, where chyme from the stomach is mixed with bile and pancreatic juice. Its diagnostic microscopic feature is the Brunner glands in the submucosa, which secrete alkaline mucus.
features: Leaf-shaped villi with crypts of Lieberkühn at their bases
Brunner glands in the submucosa, mucus-secreting clusters that mark the duodenum
Goblet cells in the villus epithelium, stained magenta with PAS
Tall columnar absorptive cells with a brush border lining the villi
Coeliac disease changes: flattened villi, crypt hyperplasia and raised intraepithelial lymphocytes

tissues.name: Jejunum
tissues.summary: The jejunum is the middle section of the small intestine and its main absorptive region. Its mucosa forms tall villi on prominent circular folds, which greatly increase the surface area for absorbing nutrients.
features: Tall finger-like villi on high circular folds (plicae circulares)
Columnar enterocytes with a brush border of microvilli
Goblet cells, and Paneth cells with red granules at the crypt bases
Lacteals in the villus cores, which absorb dietary fat
Few Peyer patches and no Brunner glands in the submucosa, which separates it from the duodenum

images.title: Crypt with Paneth cells at its base and goblet cells
images.description: H&E view of a single crypt of the small intestine. Paneth cells sit at the base with bright red cytoplasmic granules, and pale goblet cells with mucus-filled vacuoles sit among the columnar cells above them. No magnification is given in the source.

images.title: Intestinal villi lined by tall columnar cells
images.description: Phone photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece, showing intestinal mucosa cut lengthwise with long villi lined by tall columnar cells. The stain looks like H&E (pink and purple), and no magnification is given. The picture is small and soft, but a student can see the lining cells and the dense lamina propria in the core of each villus.
images.author: Rahaf Mahmoud

images.title: Intestinal mucosa with long villi projecting into a lumen
images.description: Microscope photograph of intestinal mucosa with long, narrow villi projecting into a pale lumen at the upper left. The image is soft and dark, and the stain is not stated, though the purple colouring suggests H&E. Students can see the dense, dark-nucleated cells filling the villi.
images.author: Ciência e Saúde XXI

images.title: Intestinal lining with villi and glands, photographed through an eyepiece
images.description: A phone photograph through a microscope eyepiece of a pink-stained section, with no magnification given. The field shows finger-like villi along the top and many round gland profiles (crypts) below, which looks like the mucosa of the small intestine rather than smooth muscle. The source gives only the word 'Tissue', so this image belongs with the small intestine, most likely the jejunum.
images.author: Naz Amann

tissues.name: Ileum
tissues.summary: The ileum is the final part of the small intestine, lying between the jejunum and the caecum. It absorbs bile acids and vitamin B12 bound to intrinsic factor, and its wall carries Peyer's patches that sample luminal antigens for the immune system.
features: Peyer's patches: aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa, with no villi over them
M cells: thin epithelial cells with few microvilli over the follicles, sampling luminal antigens
Goblet cells: numerous pale, mucus-filled cells among the columnar epithelium
Shorter villi than the jejunum, with crypts of Lieberkühn at their bases
Brush border of tall columnar absorptive cells lining each villus

images.title: Goblet cells in cross-section of intestinal epithelium
images.description: Section through many units of intestinal epithelium (villi or glands) cut across, with pale rounded cells around the rim of each unit that look like goblet cells. The stain appears pink and purple, probably H&E, and the source gives neither a stain nor a magnification. Students should find the goblet cells at the rim and the lamina propria core at the centre of each unit.
images.author: Author not recorded on Wikimedia Commons (see source page)

images.title: Terminal ileum villi in section, with a goblet cell arrowed
images.description: Section through terminal ileal villi, which the source calls a cross-section and stains with H&E, with an arrow marking a goblet cell in the epithelium. No magnification is given and the image is small and low resolution. Students should find the tall columnar epithelium, the arrowed goblet cell and the lamina propria in the core of the villus.

tissues.name: Colon & rectum
tissues.summary: The colon, or large intestine, absorbs water and electrolytes and stores and propels faeces, with the rectum as its final segment. Its mucosa has no villi and is lined by straight crypts packed with mucus-secreting goblet cells.
features: No villi: a flat surface with straight, tubular crypts of Lieberkühn
Goblet cells in the crypts and surface, seen as clear mucin-filled vacuoles
Tall absorptive columnar cells with basal nuclei covering the surface
Lamina propria packed with lymphocytes, sometimes forming lymphoid aggregates
Thick muscularis externa, with its longitudinal layer gathered into taeniae coli
Ano-rectal junction, where simple columnar rectal epithelium gives way to stratified squamous anal epithelium

images.title: Lymphoid aggregate in the colon wall, with crypts around it
images.description: Section of colon showing a large, densely packed lymphoid aggregate in the mucosa, just beneath the surface epithelium, with round crypt profiles around its edge. The aggregate is made of crowded small dark nuclei, most likely lymphocytes, and it appears H&E-stained. Students should find the boundary between the aggregate and the surrounding crypts, and note how the nuclei differ in density from the crypt lining.

images.title: Colon mucosa through a microscope eyepiece: straight crypts
images.description: Photograph taken through a microscope eyepiece, showing a circular field of colon mucosa that appears H&E-stained, with a crack in the section and glare across part of it. The long vertical structures with pale lumens are straight crypts, not villi, even though the source caption calls them villi and the colon has none. Students should use this image to see the crypt lumens running down through the mucosa.
images.author: Виноградова Анастасия Витальевна

images.title: Colon crypts in cross section: evenly spaced, round profiles
images.description: Circular view of normal human colon with crypts cut in cross section, each a ring of cells around a pale lumen. The source describes the crypts as an evenly spaced bed of flowers and notes that the pattern stays regular even in tangential sections. The stain is not named in the source, but it appears H&E, and students should count the goblet cells in each crypt ring.
images.author: Taraali4

images.title: Goblet cell in a canine colonoid monolayer (scanning electron micrograph)
images.description: Scanning electron micrographs with no stain, showing a goblet cell opening at the surface of a monolayer grown from canine colonoids, which come from the colon rather than the ileum. Panel C is at low power with a 5 µm bar, and panel D is a close-up with a 1 µm bar showing the goblet cell orifice (GO), a fenestrated membrane (FM) and microvilli (MV). It is useful for goblet cell surface structure but does not show ileal tissue.
images.author: Ambrosini YM, Park Y, Jergens AE, Shin W, Min S, Atherly T, et al.

tissues.name: Vermiform appendix
tissues.summary: The vermiform appendix is a narrow, blind-ended outpouching of the caecum with colon-type mucosa packed with lymphoid tissue. Its lymphoid follicles make it an immune organ, most prominent in children and young adults.
features: Colon-type mucosa: sparse, irregular crypts with goblet cells and no villi
Large lymphoid follicles in the mucosa and submucosa, often with pale germinal centres
Lumen often irregular or star-shaped in cross-section, between thick mucosal folds
Complete outer longitudinal muscle layer, not gathered into bands

images.title: Appendix mucosa with crypts and dense lymphoid tissue
images.description: Eyepiece photograph of a stained section of the vermiform appendix, with an H and E type stain (pink and purple). The source gives no magnification. Students should find the crypts (intestinal glands) set within dense lymphoid tissue, a large lymphoid aggregate in the centre of the field, and paler connective tissue at the upper right.
images.author: Abdulrazakca

tissues.name: Anal canal
tissues.summary: The terminal part of the alimentary canal, running from the rectum to the anal verge. Its lining changes from simple columnar colorectal mucosa, through a transitional zone, to non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium and then keratinised skin at the anal verge, and the internal and external sphincters control continence.
features: Simple columnar colorectal mucosa above the pectinate line, with crypts and goblet cells
Transitional zone around the pectinate line, where columnar and squamous epithelium meet
Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium below the pectinate line
Keratinised skin with hair follicles and apocrine sweat glands at the anal verge
Thick internal sphincter of smooth muscle inside the external sphincter of skeletal muscle
Internal haemorrhoidal venous plexus in the submucosa above the pectinate line

images.title: Coronal section through the anal canal and sphincters
images.description: Line drawing of a coronal section through the anal canal, shown without any stain and with no magnification given. The labelled bladder, ductus deferens and seminal vesicle place it in the pelvis, with the rectum leading down to the anal canal. Students should find the internal sphincter (smooth muscle) lying inside the external sphincter (skeletal muscle), with the levator ani alongside.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

images.title: Lower rectum and anal wall with dilated haemorrhoidal veins
images.description: Line drawing of the lower rectum and anus, with the mucous membrane removed on one side to show the veins (no stain and no magnification given). The dilated veins pass through the muscular wall to join the external haemorrhoidal plexus, and the internal and external sphincters are labelled beneath them. Students should find the columns and valve of Morgagni and Hilton's white line on the mucosal side, and the change to skin at the anal margin.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Liver
tissues.summary: The liver is the body's main metabolic and detoxifying organ. Hepatocytes form plates between blood-filled sinusoids that run from portal triads to central veins, and they secrete bile into canaliculi that drain towards the portal triads.
features: Classic lobule: central vein with radiating hepatocyte plates
Portal triad: portal venule, hepatic arteriole and bile ductule
Sinusoids lined by fenestrated endothelium and Kupffer cells
Stellate (Ito) cells in the space of Disse, which drive fibrosis in cirrhosis
Zone 3 (around the central vein) is most vulnerable to hypoxia and paracetamol toxicity

images.title: Liver hepatocytes beside fibrous connective tissue
images.description: Liver tissue from a gallbladder resection, stained with H&E; the source gives no magnification. Sheets of hepatocytes with round central nuclei and pale cytoplasm lie below a band of dense pink fibrous connective tissue containing scattered spindle-shaped cells. Students should find the hepatocyte sheets, the fibrous septum and a small vessel with red blood cells at the top left.

images.title: Diagram of a liver sinusoid and its cells
images.description: Schematic of part of a liver lobule, showing a sinusoid running from a portal venule branch on the left to a central venule on the right, with blood-flow arrows. The labels are in Hebrew and mark Kupffer cells, hepatocytes, the bile canaliculus and the space of Disse. Students should find the sinusoid lined by Kupffer cells and the hepatocytes beside it.

images.title: Hepatocytes and sinusoids at high power
images.description: Photograph through a microscope of human liver, showing hepatocytes with round nuclei arranged in cords, with pale sinusoidal spaces between them. It appears to be H&E-stained, and the source gives no magnification; a dark rod-shaped object at the upper left is not tissue. Students should find the sinusoids as the pale channels between the cords and the nuclei within the hepatocytes.
images.author: Jpogi at Wikipedia

tissues.name: Gallbladder & bile ducts
tissues.summary: The gallbladder is a muscular sac under the liver that stores bile and concentrates it by absorbing water and salts. Its mucosa is a folded simple columnar epithelium with no goblet cells, lying over a thin smooth muscle wall with no submucosa.
features: Tall simple columnar epithelium with a brush border and no goblet cells
Mucosal folds (rugae) with epithelium covering a loose lamina propria core
No submucosa: lamina propria lies directly on a thin smooth muscle layer
Thin smooth muscle wall with no muscularis mucosae
Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses (chronic cholecystitis): mucosa herniating through the muscle

images.title: Gallbladder mucosal folds over smooth muscle, H&E
images.description: Haemalum-eosin (H&E) section of the gallbladder wall, with no magnification given. Branching folds of tall columnar epithelium project into the lumen, each with a loose connective tissue core, and a band of smooth muscle lies below them with blood vessels in the lower stroma. Students should look for the tall lining cells on the folds and the thin muscle layer beneath the mucosa.
images.author: User:Polarlys

tissues.name: Exocrine pancreas
tissues.summary: The exocrine pancreas is a gland of serous acini that secrete digestive enzymes and bicarbonate-rich fluid into a duct system leading to the duodenum. Scattered among the acini are endocrine islets of Langerhans, which release insulin and glucagon into the blood.
features: Acinar cells in grape-like clusters, with basal basophilia and apical eosinophilic zymogen granules
Centroacinar cells: small, pale cells at the centre of each acinus, where the duct begins
Islets of Langerhans: pale clusters of cells with round nuclei, scattered among the acini
Interlobular connective tissue septa dividing the gland into lobules
No striated ducts (unlike the parotid gland)

images.title: Diagram of an acinus with centroacinar cells (German labels)
images.description: Colour-coded schematic, not a photograph, of one pancreatic acinus (green acinar cells) continuing into an intercalated duct (red), with centroacinar cells (red) sitting at the mouth of the acinus. The labels are in German, and the drawing matches the other two translated versions in this set. Students should find the acinus, the intercalated duct and the centroacinar cells at the junction.
images.author: Mikael Häggström

images.title: Diagram of an acinus with centroacinar cells (Spanish labels)
images.description: Colour-coded schematic, not a photograph, of one pancreatic acinus (green acinar cells) continuing into an intercalated duct (red), with centroacinar cells (red) sitting at the mouth of the acinus. The labels are in Spanish, and the drawing matches the German and Chinese versions in this set. Students should find the acinus, the intercalated duct and the centroacinar cells at the junction.
