tissues.name: Cornea
tissues.summary: The cornea is the transparent, avascular front of the eye, and it provides most of the eye's focusing power. It is a non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium over a stroma of regularly stacked collagen lamellae, with Bowman layer above and Descemet membrane and a single-layer endothelium below.
features: Non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium on the surface, with no keratin layer
Bowman layer: a thin acellular band just beneath the epithelium
Stroma: broad layer of regular collagen lamellae with flattened keratocyte nuclei between them
Descemet membrane: a sharply outlined basement membrane behind the stroma
Single endothelial layer behind Descemet membrane: does not regenerate, so losing cells causes oedema

images.title: Corneal stroma in a low-power section, eyepiece photo
images.description: Eyepiece photo of a pink-stained cornea section at low power, a curved strip of tissue with a fold at the top left and a dark thread across the right edge. Fine streaks run along the length of the strip, which is typical of stroma. The stain is not stated and looks like H&E, and no magnification is given.
images.author: Abdulrazakca

images.title: Engraved vertical section of the human cornea
images.description: Engraved line drawing of a vertical section through the human cornea, a figure from Gray's Anatomy (per the file name), with stippling that shows the layered stroma. Numbered labels run from the epithelium at the top to the endothelium at the bottom, and lettered marks sit on the stroma; the legend is not in the image. Students should compare the thin top and bottom layers with the broad stroma between them.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

images.title: Dividing human corneal cells, 1882 engraved plate
images.description: Historical engraved plate from 1882 with figures 71 to 73, showing dividing cells from the human cornea, which the source says were drawn from chromic acid-safranin preparations. Figure 71 shows a group of cells, one with a spiky chromosome figure and others with clumped chromosomes, and Figures 72 and 73 show close-up dividing cells. The source calls it possibly the oldest drawing of human chromosomes, and no magnification is given.
images.author: Walther Flemming. Professor der Anatomie in Kiel.

images.title: Corneal cross section with epithelium, elastic laminae and endothelium
images.description: Labelled line drawing of a full corneal cross section, with the epithelium at the top and the endothelium at the bottom. The anterior and posterior elastic laminae bound the thick substantia propria, whose wavy, layered fibres run through the middle. This is a cornea, not an aortic wall, so the image is misfiled.
images.author: Henry Vandyke Carter

tissues.name: Retina
tissues.summary: The retina is the thin, layered neural tissue lining the back of the eye, where photoreceptors convert light into electrical signals. Those signals pass through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons leave the eye as the optic nerve.
features: Pigment epithelium: dark brown-black layer at the outer edge, behind the photoreceptors
Photoreceptor layer: pink striped band of rod and cone outer segments
Outer nuclear layer: dense band of dark rod and cone nuclei
Inner nuclear layer: dark nuclei of bipolar, horizontal and amacrine cells
Ganglion cell layer: large pale nuclei, with nerve fibres running to the optic disc
Fovea: cones only, with the inner layers pushed aside

images.title: Mammalian retina in green fluorescence, 40x
images.description: Section of mammalian retina imaged at 40x under green fluorescence (FITC filter), with the stain not named in the source. The dark rounded profiles are most likely cell nuclei, and the brighter bands between them are probably the plexiform layers, so the image shows the layered arrangement rather than individual cell types. Students should look for the rows of dark nuclei that form the retina's nuclear layers, separated by brighter bands.
images.author: DavidChoi

images.title: Cajal's schematic drawing of the mammalian retina
images.description: Hand-drawn schematic of the mammalian retina by Santiago Ramón y Cajal, with the Spanish legend numbering the layers 1 to 9 from the rods and cones to the inner limiting membrane. It shows the neuron types in their layers (photoreceptors, bipolar, horizontal, amacrine and ganglion cells) as drawings rather than a micrograph. A student can follow the connections from the rods and cones down through the bipolar cells to the ganglion cells.
images.author: Santiago Ramón y Cajal

images.title: Low-power retina section with layers labelled
images.description: Small, low-resolution section of the eye wall, with the vitreous at the top and the sclera at the bottom. The pink and purple colours suggest H&E, though the source does not name the stain, and printed labels mark the vitreous, retina, ganglion cells, photoreceptors, choroid and sclera. A student should locate the dark band of ganglion cell nuclei above the photoreceptor layer, with the choroid and sclera beneath it.
images.author: Author not recorded on Wikimedia Commons (see source page)

images.title: Rod photoreceptor structure and the layers of the retina
images.description: Multi-panel teaching figure with a toluidine blue vertical section of the retina (panel A), a schematic of a rod (panel B) and electron micrographs of its connecting cilium, outer segment discs, pigment epithelium and synaptic ribbon (panels C to H). Some labels are in Ukrainian, and the scale bars give the scale rather than a stated magnification. A student should trace the rod from the pigment epithelium through the outer segment, connecting cilium and inner segment to its synapse, and match each part to the layers in panel A.
images.author: Nathalie Falk, Marlene Lösl, Nadja Schröder and Andreas Gießl

images.title: Schematic of retinal layers, neurons and the choroidal capillaries
images.description: Labelled schematic of the retina with light arriving from the left (arrows), so the nerve fibre layer and ganglion cells sit at the front and the rods, cones and the choroid's capillary layer at the back. It shows the cell types in their layers (ganglion, amacrine, bipolar and horizontal cells, plus rods and cones), with the labels in Polish. A student should trace the route from the photoreceptors through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, with horizontal and amacrine cells linking the pathway sideways.
images.author: Author Pancrat

images.title: Nine types of retinal ganglion cell labelled with GFP
images.description: Research figure showing GFP-labelled retinal ganglion cells from rd1 retinas at 18 months of age, with nine cell types in separate panels. Each panel shows a cell body with a branching dendritic tree, its dendritic diameter and percentage stratification, and an arrow marking the axon of the representative cell. The small insets show how deep the dendrites sit in the inner plexiform layer, which helps a student see how ganglion cell types differ.
images.author: Lin B, Peng EB

images.title: Retinal ganglion cell wiring to amacrine cells, with electron micrographs
images.description: A wiring diagram (A) and false-coloured electron micrographs (B to D) of retinal cells, showing an amacrine cell (red) linked to ganglion cells (yellow) by a gap junction (C) and a synapse (D). The source gives scale bars of 5 µm and 500 nm but no magnification. These cells are in the retina, not in the nerve ganglia, so the image belongs to the retina tissue.
images.author: Marc RE, Sigulinsky CL, Pfeiffer RL, Emrich D, Anderson JR and Jones BW

images.title: Starburst amacrine cell dendrites: input and output zones in the retina
images.description: A labelled drawing of a starburst amacrine cell in the retina, not a microscope image. Panel a shows excitatory and inhibitory input zones with the synaptic outputs around them, and panel b shows four output quadrants, each inhibiting a direction-selective ganglion cell. It belongs to the retina tissue.
images.author: Acarón Ledesma, H., Ding, J., Oosterboer, S. et al.

images.title: Computer models of two retinal ganglion cell types, monostratified and bistratified
images.description: Computer reconstructions, not microscope images, of two retinal ganglion cell types: A2 (monostratified, dendritic field 320 µm, soma 20 µm) and D1 (bistratified, dendritic field 144 µm, soma 12 µm). The lower panel shows where the dendrites sit in the inner plexiform layer and ganglion cell layer, and the image belongs to the retina tissue.
images.author: Paknahad, J., Loizos, K., Yue, L. et al.

images.title: Tracings and confocal images of recorded retinal ganglion cell types
images.description: Black-and-white traced reconstructions (A to D) and green confocal images (E to G) of recorded retinal ganglion cells, with types labelled A, B, C, D, ON, OFF and ON-OFF. Recorded cells are filled green with Alexa 488, other cells in the ganglion cell and inner nuclear layers are red from propidium iodide, and the scale bars are 100 µm. The image belongs to the retina tissue.
images.author: Hadjinicolaou AE, Cloherty SL, Hung Y-S, Kameneva T, Ibbotson MR

images.title: Wiring diagram of the AII amacrine cell network in the retina
images.description: A wiring diagram, not a microscope image, of the AII amacrine cell network in the retina, showing glutamate, dopamine, GABA, glycine and peptide inputs and outputs to OFF bipolar cells and two classes of OFF ganglion cells. The image belongs to the retina tissue, since the layers shown (photoreceptors to ganglion cell layer) are retinal.
images.author: Marc RE, Anderson JR, Jones BW, Sigulinsky CL and Lauritzen JS

tissues.name: Eyeball, lens & eyelid
tissues.summary: The walls and lens of the eyeball, together with the eyelids: a fibrous sclera continuous with the cornea, the pigmented uvea (iris, ciliary body and choroid), the transparent lens and the protective eyelids. The ciliary body secretes aqueous humour, and the lens helps focus light onto the retina.
features: Sclera: dense irregular collagenous connective tissue, continuous with the transparent cornea
Ciliary body: ciliary muscle and ciliary processes that secrete aqueous humour
Iris: pigmented stroma with sphincter and dilator pupillae muscles
Lens: thick capsule, a single layer of anterior cuboidal epithelium and anucleate lens fibres
Eyelid: tarsal plate with meibomian glands, orbicularis oculi and conjunctiva with goblet cells

tissues.name: Inner ear & cochlea
tissues.summary: The membranous labyrinth of the inner ear houses the sensory organs of hearing and balance. Hair cells in the cochlear duct and in the utricle, saccule and semicircular ducts convert sound and head movement into nerve signals.
features: Cochlear duct lying between scala vestibuli and scala tympani
Organ of Corti on the basilar membrane under the tectorial membrane
One row of inner and three rows of outer hair cells in the organ of Corti
Stria vascularis on the outer wall of the duct, secreting potassium-rich endolymph
Maculae with otoliths (utricle, saccule); cristae ampullares in the semicircular ducts
Gaps in the hair cell rows after aminoglycoside or noise damage, with outer hair cells usually lost first

images.title: Cochlear duct in cross-section, H&E stain
images.description: A cross-section through the cochlea, shown in a virtual slide viewer whose label reads 40X, stained with H&E (pink and purple). The thin Reissner's membrane runs across the top of the cochlear duct, with dense bone of the otic capsule on either side. Students should use it to see the duct's overall shape and bony walls rather than fine cell detail; the viewer controls and a thumbnail inset are visible in the screenshot.
images.author: OpenStax College

labels.text: Dense bone of the otic capsule

images.title: Cochlea overview with organ of Corti and hair cell bundles (diagram)
images.description: A composite teaching figure: a schematic of the cochlea, a cross-section of the organ of Corti with inner and outer hair cells under the tectorial membrane, and scanning electron micrographs of hair cell bundles from the base and apex. The basal bundle (high-frequency) has shorter stereocilia than the apical bundle (low-frequency), so students should link stereocilia length to position along the cochlea. The electron micrographs are not stained sections, so no stain applies.
images.author: Kassim YM, Rosenberg DB, Das S, Wang X, Huang Z, Rahman S, et al.

images.title: Organ of Corti in cross-section and outer hair cell movement
images.description: Four panels on the organ of Corti: a schematic cross-section (A), an in vivo optical coherence tomography image of the living organ (B), and cartoons of outer hair cells at rest (C) and contracting when depolarised (D). No stain applies, as these are diagrams and an imaging scan rather than a stained section. Students should learn the layers (tectorial membrane, reticular lamina, basilar membrane) and the positions of the inner and outer hair cells, not cell detail.
images.author: Zha D, Chen F, Ramamoorthy S, Fridberger A, Choudhury N, Jacques SL, et al.

images.title: Cochlear and vestibular hair cells with their nerve endings (diagram)
images.description: A diagram comparing hair cells: on the left, cochlear inner and outer hair cells with their stereocilia, ribbon synapses, afferent and efferent nerve endings and Schwann cells; on the right, type I and type II vestibular hair cells, with the calyx wrapped around the type I cell. Students should note the calyx, the kinocilium and the afferent and efferent endings, which help tell the cell types apart. No stain applies, as this is a diagram.
images.author: Masetto S, Spaiardi P, J. Johnson S.

images.title: Gentamicin hair cell loss in a cochlear explant (fluorescence)
images.description: Fluorescence confocal micrographs of a stage P2 cochlear explant, with hair cell nuclei in green (Atoh1/nGFP) and hair cell bodies in red (myosin VI antibody). Panels B to M show the outer (ohc) and inner (ihc) hair cell rows 24 hours after gentamicin at 0, 10, 50 and 100 µg/ml, and the bar graph (N) shows hair cell counts falling sharply at 50 and 100 µg/ml. Scale bars are 100 µm (A) and 50 µm (B to M); students should look for gaps in the hair cell rows and the white arrows marking debris.
images.author: Korrapati S, Roux I, Glowatzki E, Doetzlhofer A

images.title: Cochlear nerve supply: spiral ganglion neurons and hair cell connections
images.description: A diagram plus immunofluorescence panels from a mouse cochlea showing how spiral ganglion neurons link the hair cells to the brainstem. Whole-mount panels show outer hair cells labelled for prestin (green), inner hair cells labelled for calretinin (red), and spiral ganglion neuron cell bodies labelled for NeuN (red) with nerve fibres labelled for tubulin; scale bars are 50 µm. Panel D shows the three types of type I afferent terminal (Ia, Ib, Ic) on one inner hair cell.
images.author: Pavlinkova, G.

tissues.name: Spinal cord
tissues.summary: The spinal cord is the part of the central nervous system inside the vertebral canal, carrying ascending and descending nerve tracts and housing motor neurons and reflex circuits. In cross-section, grey matter forms an H-shaped core around the central canal, surrounded by white matter tracts.
features: Anterior horns: large multipolar motor neurons with Nissl bodies in their cytoplasm
Posterior horns: the sensory input region; the substantia gelatinosa at the tip processes pain
Lateral horns (T1 to L2): preganglionic sympathetic neurons
Central canal at the centre of the grey matter, lined by ependyma
White matter tracts outside the grey matter; myelinated fibres stain blue with luxol fast blue

images.title: Spinal cord cross-section: labelled diagram and low-power section
images.description: The top half is a labelled diagram of the spinal cord in cross-section, marking the grey matter horns, central canal and white matter columns. The lower half is a low-power micrograph of a whole cross-section that appears to be H&E-stained; no magnification is given. A student should find the H-shaped grey matter around the central canal and the white matter outside it.
images.author: OpenStax

images.title: Spinal cord smear: scattered motor neurons at low power
images.description: A smear of spinal cord tissue at 40x magnification; the source does not give the stain, but the cytoplasm is purple and the nuclei dark. Several multipolar motor neurons appear as purple cell bodies with branching processes, scattered among fine fibres and many small dark glial nuclei. Students should compare the large neuron cell bodies with the much smaller, darker glial nuclei around them.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Spinal cord smear: a multipolar motor neuron at 40x
images.description: A stained smear of spinal cord at 40x magnification; the source does not name the stain. A large multipolar neuron sits in the middle of the field, with several thick processes arising from its cell body. It is surrounded by fine fibres and numerous small dark glial nuclei, so a student can trace the processes out from the cell body to see the multipolar shape.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Spinal cord smear: motor neuron with branching processes at 100x
images.description: A smear of spinal cord at 100x magnification; the source does not name the stain. A multipolar neuron sits near the centre, with a purple cell body and several tapering processes running through the surrounding fibres. Dark glial nuclei are scattered throughout, so a student can compare their small size with the neuron cell body.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Spinal cord smear: motor neuron cell body at 200x
images.description: A smear of spinal cord at 200x magnification; the source does not name the stain. A large neuron cell body sits in the centre, with thick processes leaving it in several directions and small dark glial nuclei scattered around it. At this magnification a student can see the cell body and its processes more clearly than at lower power.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Spinal cord smear: motor neuron with long processes at 200x
images.description: A smear of spinal cord at 200x magnification; the source does not name the stain. A large multipolar neuron lies in the middle, with one long process running to the left and others branching from the cell body. Small dark glial nuclei and fine fibres fill the background.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Spinal cord smear: close view of a motor neuron cell body at 400x
images.description: A smear of spinal cord at 400x magnification; the source does not name the stain. The large cell body of a neuron fills the centre, with a darker area within it and several thick processes leaving it. Small dark glial nuclei lie around the cell body.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Ependymal cells and tanycytes lining the central canal, electron micrographs
images.description: A multi-panel figure of the central canal of the mouse spinal cord, mostly electron micrographs with a few light micrograph insets using PAP immunolabelling. Ependymal cells (e) and tanycytes (t) line the canal, and the panels show cilia (c) and microvilli (v) at high magnification. Students should note the ciliated surface facing the lumen and the tight junctions between lining cells (arrows).
images.author: Meletis K, Barnabé-Heider F, Carlén M, Evergren E, Tomilin N, Shupliakov O, et al.

images.title: Transverse section of human cervical spinal cord, historical engraving
images.description: A black-and-white engraved illustration of a transverse section of the human cervical spinal cord, with numbered labels but no key; no stain or magnification is given. The grey matter horns, central canal and root fibres are drawn, with root fibres at the back (top) and front (bottom) of the cord. Students can use it to find the anterior horns with their large motor cells and the posterior horns, although the numbers cannot be matched to a key.
images.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

images.title: Transverse section of vertebrate spinal cord, simplified line drawing
images.description: A simplified black-and-white line drawing of a transverse section of vertebrate spinal cord; the species, stain and magnification are not given. Labels w, g, e and c mark parts of the section, probably white matter, grey matter, ependyma and central canal, and the grey matter is shown as a field of round cells beside the canal. The left half of the figure is blank, so it is partial or schematic and should not be read as a full section.
images.author: Unknown authorUnknown author

images.title: Ependyma: cell layer lining the ventricles, with tight junctions
images.description: Labelled teaching diagram of the ependyma, the cell layer lining the fluid-filled ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. The main panel places ependymal cells beside astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia, and the right-hand panel enlarges one ependymal cell showing its nucleus, cell processes and tight junctions. Students should be able to name each cell type and recognise the tight junctions between neighbouring ependymal cells.
images.author: explorebiology

images.title: Hypothalamic tanycytes: alpha and beta types along the third ventricle
images.description: Fluorescence micrograph of a coronal section through the adult hypothalamus at about bregma -1.5, with Hoechst nuclear stain (blue), overlaid with a schematic of the tanycyte domains. It marks the third ventricle, the ependymal cells lining it, the alpha and beta tanycyte zones with their transition zones, the median eminence, and the dorsomedial, ventromedial and arcuate nuclei. Students should see how the tanycyte subtypes are arranged along the ventricle wall and how the flanking nuclei vary with level.
images.author: Goodman T and Hajihosseini MK

tissues.name: Cerebral cortex
tissues.summary: The cerebral cortex is the thin outer layer of grey matter covering the cerebral hemispheres, where sensory information is processed, voluntary movement is planned and higher mental functions take place. Most of it is six-layered neocortex, with pyramidal and granular neurons arranged in layers and supported by glia.
features: Six layers, I (molecular) to VI (multiform), with the cell types changing from layer to layer
Layer I is cell-poor, with mostly fibres and few cell bodies
Layers II and IV are packed with small granular neurons; layers III and V hold pyramidal neurons, the largest in layer V
Layer V of the primary motor cortex contains giant Betz cells
Primary visual cortex has a thick layer IV with the stria of Gennari, a band of myelinated fibres
Glia (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia) are scattered through the neuropil, seen as small dark nuclei

images.title: Fluorescent neurons with branching dendrites above a layer of nuclei
images.description: Fluorescence image of neurons, with white-labelled cell bodies and long, branching dendrites rising above a layer of blue-stained nuclei. The source gives only 4-week-old neurons, so the labelling method, magnification and brain region are not stated. The cell bodies with a long apical dendrite resemble cortical pyramidal neurons, which makes the image useful for showing neuron shape.
images.author: Jason Snyder from Washington, DC, United States

images.title: Four glial cell types of the central nervous system, colour coded
images.description: Colour-coded teaching illustration (not a microscope image) of four central nervous system glial cells: ependymal cells in pink with cilia lining a ventricle, green astrocytes, dark red microglia and blue oligodendrocytes. A red blood vessel runs past an astrocyte near the ependymal layer. Students should learn to tell the four types apart by shape and by where they sit relative to the ventricle and blood vessels.
images.author: Artwork by Holly Fischer

images.title: Six glial cell types, grouped into central and peripheral nervous systems
images.description: Labelled teaching illustration (not a microscope image) with a key listing six glial cell types: astrocytes, microglial cells, oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells in the central nervous system, and Schwann cells and satellite glial cells in the peripheral nervous system. Each cell type is drawn as a small icon beside larger panels, with a CNS panel showing the ependymal layer, astrocytes, microglia and oligodendrocytes, and a PNS panel showing Schwann cells along nerve fibres with green satellite cells. Students should match each name to its shape and to whether it belongs to the CNS or PNS.
images.author: explorebiology

tissues.name: Cerebellum
tissues.summary: The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and motor learning, and its cortex is a tightly folded sheet of grey matter with three layers around white-matter cores called arbor vitae. Its only output is the Purkinje cell layer, which sends inhibitory (GABA) signals to the deep cerebellar nuclei.
features: Molecular layer: the outer, pale, sparsely populated layer with few stellate and basket cell nuclei
Purkinje cell layer: a single row of large flask-shaped neurons at the boundary between the molecular and granular layers
Granular layer: densely packed small dark granule cell nuclei, the most cellular layer of the cortex
Arbor vitae: the pale white-matter core of each folium
Deep nuclei such as the dentate: larger, scattered neurons among fibres in the white matter

images.title: Cerebellar cortex: granular and molecular layers in H&E
images.description: H&E-stained cerebellar cortex showing the dense, dark granular layer on the left and the pale pink molecular layer on the right. Two large Purkinje cells, marked by arrows, sit at the border between the two layers. The printed labels on the picture are in German, and the source gives no magnification.
images.author: Sbrandner

images.title: Purkinje cells and their dendrites in a silver stain at 200x
images.description: Silver-impregnated cerebellar cross-section at 200x magnification, showing a curved row of large brown Purkinje cell bodies between the dense granular layer and the molecular layer. The black silver-stained dendrites branch out into the molecular layer. Students should look for the single row of Purkinje cells and their branching dendritic trees.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

images.title: Purkinje cells in luxol fast blue and cresyl violet stain at 400x
images.description: Cerebellar cross-section at 400x magnification stained with luxol fast blue and cresyl violet. Two large Purkinje cell bodies sit at the edge of the dense blue granular layer, with the sparser molecular layer and its scattered glial nuclei on the pale left side. Students should note how the large Purkinje cells stand out from the small, tightly packed granule cell nuclei.
images.author: Berkshire Community College Bioscience Image Library

tissues.name: Hippocampus
tissues.summary: The hippocampus proper is a three-layered archicortex in the medial temporal lobe that is essential for forming new declarative memories. Its principal cells are the CA pyramidal neurons and dentate granule cells, and CA1 is especially vulnerable to hypoxia.
features: CA1 (Sommer sector): a dense band of pyramidal neurons lying next to the subiculum
CA fields: pyramidal cell layer with stratum oriens on one side and stratum radiatum on the other
Dentate gyrus granule cell layer: a tightly packed, V- or U-shaped band of small round neurons
Hilus: scattered larger neurons inside the fold of the granule cell layer
Molecular layer: cell-poor neuropil outside the granule cells, towards the hippocampal fissure
Alveus and fimbria: white fibre tracts running over the surface of the CA fields

images.title: Golgi's historical plate of the hippocampus
images.description: A sepia plate labelled C. Golgi, showing the curved hippocampus in section with fine radiating fibres and groups of cells. The source gives no description, magnification or stain; the plate probably shows Golgi-stained tissue, since Golgi developed the silver method. Students can use it to compare the classic hippocampal outline with modern stained sections.
images.author: Camillo Golgi

images.title: Hippocampal regions CA1, CA3 and dentate gyrus, labelled
images.description: A low-power photograph of a hippocampal section with CA1, CA3 and dentate gyrus (DG) labelled on the image, showing the hooked outline of the hippocampus. The source gives no stain or magnification, and the section looks mauve-pink. Students should use it as a map to match each named region with the cell layers in the higher-power images.
images.author: Author not recorded on Wikimedia Commons (see source page)

images.title: Subgranular zone: stem cells, precursors and granule neurons (diagram)
images.description: A colour schematic, not a micrograph, of a section through the subgranular zone of the dentate gyrus. It shows neural stem cells giving rise, through transit amplifying precursors and neuroblasts, to granule neurons, with astrocytes and a blood vessel nearby, and a legend identifies each cell type. Students should learn to recognise these cell types and their order in the lineage that produces new granule neurons in the adult dentate gyrus.
images.author: Ilias Kazanis, Justin Lathia, Lara Moss, Charles ffrench-Constant

images.title: Proliferating cells in the dentate gyrus and rostral migratory stream
images.description: A four-panel immunofluorescence figure from Faiz et al. (BMC Neuroscience, 2005). Panels a and b show the rostral migratory stream, and panels c to e show the dentate gyrus, with BrdU (red) marking cells that were proliferating and nestin or GFAP (green) marking progenitors and glial filaments. The subgranular zone (sgz) and dentate gyrus (dg) are labelled, and scale bars of 25, 50 and 10 micrometres are given but no magnification.
images.author: Maryam Faiz , Laia Acarin , Bernardo Castellano and Berta Gonzalez

images.title: Coronal brain section through the hippocampus, labelled
images.description: A low-power, labelled coronal section of the brain with the hippocampus at the lower right, where CA1, CA3, dentate gyrus (DG), subiculum (SB) and fimbria (FI) are marked. Many thalamic nuclei and cortical areas are also labelled elsewhere on the section. The source gives no stain or magnification, but the purple cell bodies suggest a Nissl-type stain, so students should use it to place the hippocampus within the brain rather than to study cell detail.
images.author: Brain Maps.org

images.title: Enlarged crop of proliferating cells in the dentate gyrus
images.description: A crop of the same Faiz et al. 2005 figure, showing panels c to e: BrdU (red) with nestin or GFAP (green) in the dentate gyrus, with the dg and sgz labelled. It repeats the content of the full four-panel figure at a larger size, so it is a duplicate of that entry.
images.author:
Phenotypes_of_proliferating_cells_in_the_Rostral_Migratory_Stream_and_Dentate_Gyrus.jpg: Maryam Faiz , Laia Acarin , Bernardo Castellano and Berta Gonzalez
derivative work: CopperKettle (talk)

tissues.name: Brainstem & basal ganglia
tissues.summary: The brainstem (midbrain, pons and medulla) contains cranial nerve nuclei and pigmented nuclei such as the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus, threaded with myelinated tracts. The basal ganglia, including the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen), are deep grey matter nuclei that help control movement.
features: Neuromelanin: brown granular cytoplasm in substantia nigra and locus coeruleus neurons
Pontine nuclei: granular neuropil of small neurons, divided by blue myelinated fibre bundles
Cranial nerve motor nuclei: clusters of large multipolar neurons beside the fourth ventricle
Striatum (caudate and putamen): pink neuropil crossed by myelinated fibre bundles
Locus coeruleus: pigmented neurons in the lateral floor of the fourth ventricle

tissues.name: Meninges & choroid plexus
tissues.summary: The meninges are three connective tissue layers (dura, arachnoid and pia mater) that enclose the brain and spinal cord. The choroid plexus is a highly vascular structure projecting into the brain ventricles that secretes cerebrospinal fluid, and its epithelial cells are joined by tight junctions that form the blood-CSF barrier.
features: Dura: dense, collagen-rich fibrous connective tissue forming the outer layer
Arachnoid: thin sheet with delicate trabeculae crossing the subarachnoid space
Pia: thin layer adhering closely to the surface of the brain or spinal cord
Choroid plexus: fronds of fenestrated capillaries covered by cuboidal epithelium with microvilli
Choroid plexus epithelial cells joined by tight junctions, forming the blood-CSF barrier
Arachnoid cap cells, the origin of meningiomas, which may contain psammoma bodies
